Hyperventilation would need a faster or deeper pattern, and hypoventilation raises ETCO2. Partial obstruction changes the waveform shape, and the right response here is to treat the circulation.

questions.stem: During sedation, complete laryngospasm abruptly stops airflow. Which standard monitor should reflect the loss of ventilation first?
options: Capnography
Pulse oximetry
ECG rate and rhythm
Precordial stethoscope
questions.explanation: Capnography shows the loss of airflow on the next breath, because no exhaled CO2 reaches the sampling line. Pulse oximetry lags by a minute or more, especially with supplemental oxygen, and ECG changes such as bradycardia appear only after hypoxemia. A precordial stethoscope is not a standard monitor.

questions.stem: The proceduralist asks to remove capnography during moderate sedation because the cannula is uncomfortable. What is the best response?
options: Remove it, since SpO2 above 95% shows safe breathing
Reposition or swap the cannula; keep CO2 monitoring
Replace it with watching chest rise every few minutes
Raise oxygen flow and stop the CO2 sampling
questions.explanation: ASA standards expect exhaled CO2 monitoring during moderate or deep sedation unless it is precluded, and discomfort is fixed by adjusting the interface, such as a different cannula or a mask with a sampling port. SpO2 on oxygen detects hypoventilation late, and intermittent visual checks of chest rise miss obstruction and apnea between looks.

questions.stem: During moderate/deep procedural sedation, blood pressure is checked only every 15 minutes despite ongoing IV sedative administration. What is the problem?
options: Fifteen minutes is acceptable when the first BP is normal
An arterial line is needed for deep sedation
The interval is too long; check at least every 5 minutes
Ten-minute checks are acceptable for moderate sedation
questions.explanation: Blood pressure is measured at least every 5 minutes during moderate and deep sedation, because sedative boluses can cause sudden hypotension. A normal starting value does not lengthen the interval, 10 minutes is still too long, and noninvasive measurement is acceptable for most cases.

questions.stem: Two sedated patients both have ETCO2 58 mmHg; one is bradypneic and the other has rapid shallow breathing. What common physiologic problem can produce both patterns?
options: Increased metabolic CO2 production
Rebreathing of exhaled CO2
Hyperventilation from pain
Inadequate alveolar ventilation
questions.explanation: ETCO2 in a spontaneously breathing patient reflects alveolar ventilation, which is tidal volume minus dead space times rate. A slow rate lowers it directly, and rapid shallow breaths waste a larger fraction of each breath on dead space, so both reduce alveolar ventilation. Increased CO2 production or rebreathing could raise ETCO2 but do not explain both breathing patterns.

questions.stem: A deeply sedated patient receiving nasal oxygen becomes apneic. Which sequence is expected?
options: Capnogram flattens now; SpO2 may hold for minutes
SpO2 falls first; the capnogram changes later
Both change within the same few seconds
ETCO2 stays normal until desaturation begins
questions.explanation: The capnogram flattens at the onset of apnea because exhaled CO2 stops reaching the sampling port, while SpO2 holds for minutes on supplemental oxygen as the alveolar reserve is consumed. That lag is why capnography, not oximetry, is the early apnea monitor during sedation.

questions.stem: Which TWO bedside measures most directly assess ventilation during spontaneous-breathing sedation? (Select 2)
options: Pulse oximetry on supplemental oxygen
Plethysmograph waveform amplitude
Heart rate response to stimulation
Observed respiratory rate and depth
Capnography waveform/trend
Bispectral index value
questions.explanation: Capnography and the observed rate and depth of breathing assess ventilation directly. Pulse oximetry on supplemental oxygen can stay normal while CO2 rises, the plethysmograph reflects perfusion, and BIS and heart rate reflect sedation depth and sympathetic tone rather than ventilation.

questions.stem: During MAC, ETCO2 rises and respiratory rate slows after propofol plus opioid administration while SpO2 remains normal. Which mechanism is most likely?
options: Partial upper-airway obstruction by the tongue
Cumulative synergistic respiratory depression
CO2 rebreathing under tented surgical drapes
Opioid-induced chest wall rigidity
questions.explanation: Propofol and opioids act synergistically on respiratory drive, so their combined effect is greater than either alone, and a slowing rate with rising ETCO2 is central depression. Obstruction usually brings snoring or paradoxical effort rather than a slow rate, rebreathing raises the baseline rather than slowing breathing, and rigidity follows large rapid opioid doses.

questions.stem: MAC converts to general anesthesia with an LMA connected to the anesthesia machine ventilator. Beyond capnography and pulse oximetry, which monitors are now required? (Select 2)
options: Processed EEG monitor
Arterial line for blood gases
Inspired oxygen analyzer with low alarm
Precordial stethoscope
Esophageal temperature probe
Breathing circuit disconnect alarm
questions.explanation: Once general anesthesia is delivered through a breathing system, ASA standards require an inspired oxygen analyzer with a low-concentration alarm and, when a ventilator is used, a circuit disconnect alarm. Processed EEG and arterial lines are added by indication, a precordial stethoscope is optional, and temperature is monitored when a significant change is anticipated.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with CAD undergoes deep sedation for cardioversion. Why is continuous ECG particularly appropriate?
options: ECG replaces pulse oximetry during deep sedation
Capnography makes ECG redundant in deep sedation
Depth and CAD both raise ischemia and rhythm risk
The shock removes arrhythmia risk afterward
questions.explanation: ECG monitoring is tied to sedation depth and cardiac risk, and deep sedation in a patient with CAD, plus a shock that can trigger arrhythmias or ischemia, makes continuous ECG essential. Post-shock bradycardia or VF can still occur. Neither pulse oximetry nor capnography detects rhythm or ST changes, so they cannot replace the ECG.

questions.stem: A patient with stable COPD has baseline ETCO2 around 50 mmHg. During MAC, what is most useful for detecting respiratory deterioration?
options: SpO2, since COPD makes ETCO2 unreliable
Any ETCO2 reading above 45 mmHg
A single ETCO2 value at the case's end
Waveform and ETCO2 change from baseline
questions.explanation: Patients who retain CO2 at baseline will look abnormal against a population cutoff, so the useful signal is a change from their own baseline in value, rate, or waveform shape. Relying on SpO2 misses hypoventilation on supplemental oxygen, and a single value at the end of the case detects nothing in time.

questions.stem: Which THREE statements about pulse oximetry during sedation are correct? (Select 3)
options: It continuously assesses oxygenation
Supplemental oxygen can delay its response to hypoventilation
It does not directly measure ventilation
It detects apnea immediately
It replaces capnography
It is unnecessary during moderate sedation
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry continuously reflects oxygenation but does not measure ventilation, and on supplemental oxygen it can stay normal for minutes after hypoventilation begins. That delay is why it does not detect apnea immediately and cannot replace capnography, and it remains required at every level of sedation, including moderate.

questions.stem: During MAC, the anesthesia provider is engaged in conversation and does not notice the capnogram deteriorating. Which safety principle is most directly violated?
options: Proceduralist shares ventilation monitoring
Continuous vigilance despite distraction
Conversation itself depresses ventilation
Capnography adds little in a sleeping patient
questions.explanation: The anesthesia provider is responsible for continuous attention to ventilation, and conversation that pulls eyes off the capnogram removes the main early warning for apnea. The proceduralist is focused on the procedure and cannot share that role, and a patient who looks asleep is exactly the one who needs capnography most.

questions.stem: During TIVA, NIBP on an obese patient's upper arm reads 162/98, while an arterial line in the other arm reads 128/74. Which cuff problem best explains the difference?
options: The cuff is too wide for the arm
The arm is held above heart level
The cuff is too narrow for the arm
The transducer sits below the heart
questions.explanation: A cuff bladder that is too narrow for the arm needs extra pressure to compress the artery, so it overestimates blood pressure, a common problem in obesity. A cuff that is too wide reads low, and an arm above heart level also reads low. A transducer below the heart would make the arterial line read high, which would shrink the gap rather than explain it.

questions.stem: ECG leads are removed during MAC and not replaced for 15 minutes. Which principle is violated?
options: ECG is needed at induction and emergence
ECG can pause if SpO2 stays normal
Pulse oximetry can stand in for ECG
ECG must be displayed continuously
questions.explanation: ASA basic standards require the ECG to be continuously displayed from the start of anesthesia until the patient leaves the anesthetizing location, and MAC is included. A pulse oximeter gives a rate but cannot show rhythms such as VT or heart block, or ischemic ST changes, so a 15-minute gap leaves those undetected.

questions.stem: After a sedative bolus, which monitor usually provides the earliest objective evidence of respiratory depression?
options: Capnography rate/waveform
Pulse oximetry on supplemental oxygen
Noninvasive blood pressure trend
ECG heart rate trend
questions.explanation: Capnography reports every breath, so a slowing rate, smaller waveforms, or apnea appear within seconds of respiratory depression. Pulse oximetry on oxygen can stay normal for minutes, and blood pressure and heart rate change only after hypercapnia or hypoxemia develop.

questions.stem: Which MAC case most clearly makes temperature monitoring clinically important?
options: Brief cataract surgery under topical block
Long burn excision with large exposed areas
Twenty-minute colonoscopy in a warm room
Carpal tunnel release under a Bier block
questions.explanation: Burned skin loses its barrier against evaporative and radiant heat loss, and a long case with large exposed areas makes a clinically significant temperature drop likely, which is when temperature monitoring is expected. Short, covered procedures such as cataract surgery, a brief colonoscopy, or a hand case under IV regional rarely produce meaningful temperature change.

questions.stem: Which FOUR factors should guide sedative titration when the patient becomes too deep during low stimulation and too light during painful moments? (Select 4)
options: Changing procedural stimulus
Drug interactions
The total dose used at a prior procedure
A fixed weight-based dosing schedule
Drug kinetics
Effect-site delay
questions.explanation: Titration should account for each drug's kinetics, the delay to peak effect-site concentration, interactions such as opioid and propofol synergy, and how stimulation changes during the procedure. A fixed weight-based schedule or a prior procedure's total dose ignores these changing factors and causes overshoot or undershoot.

questions.stem: Two propofol boluses are given in rapid succession before the first has reached peak clinical effect; apnea follows. Which error occurred?
options: Slowed redistribution of propofol
Reduced hepatic propofol metabolism
Dose stacking during the onset delay
Acute tolerance to the first bolus
questions.explanation: Propofol takes about 1.5 to 2 minutes to reach peak effect at the brain, so a second bolus given before then adds to a first dose that has not yet shown its full effect, and the combined peak causes apnea. Redistribution and metabolism end a bolus's effect rather than delay its onset, and tolerance would blunt, not deepen, the response.

questions.stem: A moderately sedated patient has RR 12/min, regular capnogram morphology, and stable ETCO2 45 mmHg without a concerning trend. What is the best response?
options: Keep observing closely; no intervention yet
Give naloxone for the elevated ETCO2
Treat it as early apnea and stimulate
Lighten sedation until ETCO2 is below 40
questions.explanation: A regular waveform, a rate of 12, and a stable ETCO2 of 45 mmHg reflect the mild, expected rise in CO2 with moderate sedation, so the right move is continued close observation of the trend. Reversal or lightening to chase a number below 40 treats a value rather than a problem, and apnea would show a flat trace.

questions.stem: During MAC for a breast biopsy, the patient responds to voice and breathes comfortably. Under ASA basic monitoring standards, how must ventilation be assessed?
options: Clinical observation until responsiveness is lost
Clinical signs plus continuous exhaled CO2 monitoring
Pulse oximetry trend, since SpO2 reflects ventilation
Exhaled CO2 once deep sedation is reached
questions.explanation: ASA basic standards require that ventilation during moderate or deep sedation be evaluated by continual clinical observation and by monitoring exhaled CO2 unless the patient, procedure, or equipment prevents it. Waiting until responsiveness is lost misses early hypoventilation, and pulse oximetry measures oxygenation, which can stay normal on supplemental oxygen while CO2 climbs.

questions.stem: The nasal capnogram intermittently disappears whenever a sedated patient breathes through the mouth, while chest excursion and oxygenation remain stable. What is the likely explanation?
options: Mouth breathing signals recurrent central apnea
Nasal sampling line kinks when the jaw opens
Bronchospasm cutting off expiratory flow
Nasal sampling misses exhaled gas from the mouth
questions.explanation: A nasal sampling port captures exhaled gas from the nose, so when the patient breathes through the mouth the trace drops out even though ventilation continues, as stable chest movement and oxygenation show. Central apnea would stop chest movement, and a kinked line would not track the switch between nasal and oral breathing so closely.

questions.stem: During deep sedation, BP is measured only every 15 minutes and significant hypotension is discovered late. Which process error contributed?
options: BP checked too infrequently for the depth
Using NIBP rather than an arterial line
Cuff placed on the arm with the IV
Relying on SpO2 to flag hypotension
questions.explanation: During anesthesia care, blood pressure is evaluated at least every 5 minutes, so a 15-minute interval can let important hypotension go unrecognized after sedative boluses. An arterial line is not required for routine deep sedation, so noninvasive measurement was not the error, and SpO2 cannot serve as a blood-pressure monitor.

questions.stem: A patient who received midazolam and fentanyl for colonoscopy arrives in recovery still drowsy. When can continuous monitoring be relaxed?
options: As soon as the procedure ends and stimulation stops
After recovery criteria confirm near-baseline status
Once SpO2 is above 94% on supplemental oxygen
After a fixed 15 minutes in the recovery area
questions.explanation: Monitoring continues until the patient meets recovery criteria such as near-baseline consciousness, stable vital signs, and adequate ventilation, because respiratory depression often peaks after stimulation stops. A fixed time ignores drug and patient variation, and SpO2 on oxygen can stay normal while hypoventilation develops.

questions.stem: During sedation, the patient snores and the capnogram becomes low-amplitude and irregular rather than disappearing completely. Which problem is most likely?
options: Complete upper-airway obstruction
Opioid-induced central hypopnea
Partial upper-airway obstruction
Hyperventilation from anxiety
questions.explanation: Snoring means air is still moving through a narrowed pharynx, and the low, irregular capnogram reflects reduced, turbulent flow, so this is partial obstruction that usually responds to jaw thrust, chin lift, or a nasal airway. Complete obstruction would be silent with a flat trace, and central hypopnea is quiet rather than noisy.

questions.stem: Which FOUR resources should be immediately available where anesthesia-provider MAC is performed? (Select 4)
options: Advanced airway equipment
Suction
A volatile anesthetic vaporizer
A processed EEG monitor
Oxygen with positive-pressure ventilation capability
Emergency drugs
questions.explanation: Any location for anesthesia-provider MAC needs oxygen with a way to give positive-pressure ventilation, suction, emergency drugs, advanced airway equipment, and standard monitors including capnography. A vaporizer and processed EEG are useful in some settings but are not required minimum rescue resources.

questions.stem: During MAC for eye surgery with drapes tented over the face, the capnogram baseline rises to 6 mmHg and the patient becomes tachypneic and tachycardic. What is the most likely cause?
options: Exhausted soda lime in the machine
Hypoventilation from deeper sedation
Increased CO2 production from fever
CO2 accumulating under the drapes
questions.explanation: A baseline that no longer returns to zero means the patient is inhaling exhaled CO2, and under tented drapes with low gas flow, CO2 pools around the face and drives tachypnea and tachycardia. Raising flow under the drapes clears it. Soda lime only matters in a circle system, and hypoventilation or fever raises the peak ETCO2, not the inspired baseline.

questions.stem: RR falls to 6/min and ETCO2 rises while SpO2 remains 96% on oxygen. Why should intervention occur before desaturation?
options: Ventilation is already failing; oxygen masks it
SpO2 of 96% means desaturation is seconds away
Nasal ETCO2 overestimates PaCO2, so act early
A rate of 6/min is expected under sedation
questions.explanation: Capnography samples ventilation, whereas pulse oximetry samples oxygenation. With supplemental oxygen, apnea or severe hypoventilation can be present while SpO2 remains normal, making the capnogram an earlier warning of respiratory compromise.

questions.stem: A sedated patient receives oxygen by face mask. Which approach best assesses ventilation continuously?
options: SpO2, since the mask gives a high FiO2
Capnography sampled from a port in the mask
Watching the mask fog with each breath
Intermittent auscultation over the trachea
questions.explanation: A mask with a CO2 sampling port gives a continuous waveform and respiratory rate, so apnea or obstruction shows up within one breath. High FiO2 makes SpO2 an even later sign of hypoventilation, and fogging or intermittent auscultation is neither continuous nor quantitative. The absolute value reads low from dilution by mask flow, so follow the trend.

questions.stem: ETCO2 abruptly reads zero with an intact-appearing sampling line while pulse and SpO2 remain normal. What is the first action?
options: Replace the CO2 module before touching the patient
Raise oxygen flow and recheck in a minute
Check the patient for airflow and open the airway
Recalibrate the monitor, since SpO2 is normal
questions.explanation: With an intact sampling line, an ETCO2 of zero means no exhaled gas is reaching the sensor, so apnea or complete obstruction must be ruled out at the patient first. SpO2 can stay normal for minutes after ventilation stops, so a normal reading does not point to equipment failure. Check the equipment only after confirming the patient is breathing.

questions.stem: Why can pulse oximetry provide a dangerously late warning of respiratory depression during sedation with supplemental oxygen?
options: SpO2 tracks ventilation, not oxygenation
Probe averaging delays every SpO2 change by minutes
Rising CO2 shifts the curve and raises SpO2
Oxygen reserve delays desaturation despite apnea
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen fills the lungs with an oxygen reserve, so SpO2 can stay acceptable for minutes after ventilation fails. Rising CO2 shifts the curve to the right, which lowers rather than raises saturation, and probe averaging adds only seconds of delay.

questions.stem: A brief intensely painful biopsy and a long minimally stimulating endoscopy are planned. Which feature most directly determines the peak analgesic/sedative requirement?
options: Total duration of stimulation alone
Intensity and variability of stimulation
Total planned dose of sedative drugs
Intensity of the patient's baseline anxiety
questions.explanation: Peak drug requirement is set by how intense the most stimulating moment is and how much stimulation swings during the case, so a brief intensely painful biopsy can need more at its peak than a long, mild endoscopy. Duration affects total dose and accumulation rather than the peak, and baseline anxiety modifies need but does not set the peak.

questions.stem: Why does a procedure that cannot be rapidly paused for airway rescue make deep sedation with an unsecured airway less attractive?
options: Longer cases always require general anesthesia
Pausing a procedure lengthens recovery
Deterioration may occur while access blocks rescue
Sedation depth falls whenever a procedure pauses
questions.explanation: If the procedure cannot be stopped quickly, an airway problem may develop while the team cannot reach the airway, which makes an unsecured deep sedation plan riskier. Depth actually tends to increase, not fall, when stimulation stops, which makes that distractor the reverse of reality.

questions.stem: Which procedure is generally most compatible with sedation when patient and procedural factors are otherwise favorable?
options: Major craniotomy under full immobility
Open cholecystectomy
Flexible sigmoidoscopy
Cemented total hip arthroplasty without regional anesthesia
questions.explanation: Flexible sigmoidoscopy is short, moderately stimulating, and does not require immobility or airway sharing, so it suits sedation when the patient is a good candidate. Craniotomy, open cholecystectomy, and cemented hip arthroplasty involve intense stimulation, long duration, or physiologic stress that call for general or neuraxial anesthesia.

questions.stem: Which cardiovascular procedure often requires a brief period of deep sedation because the stimulus is intense but extremely short?
options: Ambulatory ECG placement
Routine diagnostic angiography
Pacemaker generator change under effective local anesthesia
Synchronized electrical cardioversion
questions.explanation: Cardioversion lasts seconds but is intensely stimulating, so brief deep sedation is typical. Angiograms and generator changes are usually done under lighter sedation with local.

questions.stem: Why does upper endoscopy generally create more difficult airway rescue than colonoscopy at the same sedation depth?
options: EGD is usually the longer procedure
EGD is usually the more painful procedure
EGD requires prone positioning
The scope shares and blocks the airway
questions.explanation: During EGD the endoscope occupies the pharynx, so mask ventilation, jaw thrust, and airway adjuncts are blocked until the scope is removed, and secretions add obstruction risk. Colonoscopy leaves the airway free. EGD is usually shorter than colonoscopy, not longer, and it is done supine or lateral rather than prone.

questions.stem: During awake craniotomy, which procedural requirement most constrains sedative depth?
options: The patient must cooperate with neurologic testing
The head is pinned and turned from the provider
Scalp blocks may be incomplete
Cortical stimulation may trigger seizures
questions.explanation: During awake craniotomy, the patient must be awake enough to speak and move on command for mapping, which limits sedative depth. Pinning and head position limit airway access, incomplete scalp blocks raise analgesic needs, and seizures are a complication, but none of these is the main limit on depth.

questions.stem: Which TWO MRI characteristics most increase anesthetic risk during sedation? (Select 2)
options: Need for neuromuscular blockade
Intense noxious stimulation during scanning
Need for prolonged immobility
Large fluid shifts during the scan
Restricted physical access to the airway/patient in the scanner environment
High risk of surgical bleeding
questions.explanation: MRI requires a still patient for long periods and places the patient inside a bore away from the anesthesia provider, limiting airway access during sedation. Scanning itself is not painful, neuromuscular blockade is unnecessary for sedation, and fluid shifts are minimal, so those are not the main hazards.

questions.stem: A laterally positioned sedated patient develops worsening oxygenation. Which change can contribute?
options: Nondependent-lung compression lowers FRC
Dependent-lung compression lowers FRC
The dependent lung gains FRC from gravity
Perfusion shifts to the nondependent lung
questions.explanation: In the lateral position, the dependent lung is compressed by the mediastinum and abdominal contents, lowering its FRC and compliance, while gravity sends more perfusion to that same lung. The resulting V/Q mismatch worsens oxygenation under sedation. Perfusion shifts toward rather than away from the dependent lung.

questions.stem: During beach-chair MAC, systemic hypotension develops. Which positioning-related consequence is most concerning?
options: Brain perfusion pressure is higher than the cuff shows
The upright position eliminates obstruction risk
Brain perfusion pressure is lower than the cuff shows
Dependent-lung atelectasis worsens oxygenation
questions.explanation: In the beach-chair position the brain sits well above an arm cuff, so hydrostatic pressure makes arterial pressure at brain level lower than the cuff reading. Hypotension that looks moderate on the cuff can therefore mean cerebral hypoperfusion. The 'higher than the cuff' option reverses the direction of the gradient.

questions.stem: During a prolonged prone operation, which combination most increases postoperative visual-loss risk?
options: A short prone case on a horseshoe headrest
A lateral case with moderate blood loss
A long supine case with stable hemoglobin
Major blood loss with long prone time
questions.explanation: Postoperative visual loss after prone surgery is linked most to long prone duration and large blood loss, along with anemia, obesity, and the Wilson frame, which raise venous pressure and lower optic nerve perfusion. Short prone cases, supine cases, and moderate blood loss carry much lower risk.

questions.stem: Which THREE measures help reduce postoperative visual-loss risk in prolonged prone surgery? (Select 3)
options: Deliberate hypotension to limit blood loss
Crystalloid alone to replace large blood loss
Keep the head neutral, level with or above the heart
Horseshoe headrest to spread facial pressure
Avoid direct pressure on the globes
Maintain adequate perfusion and oxygenation
questions.explanation: For prolonged prone spine surgery, avoiding pressure on the globes, keeping the head neutral at or above heart level, and maintaining blood pressure, hemoglobin, and oxygenation reduce the risk of ischemic optic neuropathy. Deliberate hypotension and crystalloid-only replacement of large blood loss are associated with visual loss, and a horseshoe headrest risks direct globe compression.

questions.stem: Why is prolonged prone deep sedation with an unsecured airway especially hazardous?
options: Limited airway access while edema worsens
Capnography is unreliable when prone
Prone positioning reduces FRC to zero
Prone deep sedation always requires paralysis
questions.explanation: Prone positioning limits access to the face, so repositioning the jaw, placing an airway, or intubating is slow, and facial and airway edema worsens over a long case. Deep sedation adds obstruction and apnea risk to an airway that is hard to reach. Capnography works prone, and FRC actually improves with proper support.

questions.stem: A patient with BMI 52 and severe OSA will receive deep sedation for endoscopy. Which setup best preserves oxygen reserve and airway patency?
options: Flat supine with a small head pillow
Ramped so the ear aligns with the sternal notch
Flat supine with a shoulder roll for extension
Trendelenburg to improve venous return
questions.explanation: Ramping until the external auditory meatus aligns with the sternal notch shifts abdominal weight off the diaphragm, which raises FRC and lengthens safe apnea time, and it improves mask ventilation and the laryngoscopic view if rescue is needed. A shoulder roll extends the neck but does nothing for FRC, and Trendelenburg pushes abdominal contents toward the chest.

questions.stem: Why can a 4-hour MAC create more airway risk than a 20-minute MAC in an otherwise similar patient?
options: Monitoring can be reduced after the first hour
Longer cases need less total sedative
Longer unprotected exposure and drug accumulation
Restlessness decreases as time passes
questions.explanation: A 4-hour MAC exposes the unsecured airway to obstruction for much longer, and repeated doses accumulate, especially with context-sensitive drugs. Patients often become restless from positioning discomfort, prompting more sedation and drifting deeper than intended. Longer cases need more total drug, and monitoring is not reduced over time.

questions.stem: A patient must follow commands during carotid stenting. How should this requirement influence sedation?
options: Deep sedation, waking briefly for each neuro check
Neuromuscular blockade to keep the patient still
Skip local anesthetic so discomfort keeps them alert
Keep sedation light enough for reliable neuro exams
questions.explanation: Neurologic testing during stenting, such as speech and contralateral hand grip, is the monitor for cerebral ischemia, so sedation must stay light enough that a new deficit is recognized at once. Cycling deep sedation with brief wake-ups delays detection and confuses residual drug effect with a deficit, and paralysis abolishes the exam entirely.

questions.stem: During facial surgery under MAC, supplemental oxygen accumulates beneath drapes near electrocautery. Which hazard becomes a major anesthetic concern?
options: Operating-room fire in an oxygen-enriched field
Postoperative visual loss
Hypercarbia from CO2 trapped under drapes
Corneal abrasion from drape contact
questions.explanation: Oxygen pooling under drapes near electrocautery creates the oxidizer and ignition source for a surgical fire, which makes fire the major anesthetic concern. Trapped CO2 under drapes can occur but does not carry the same catastrophic risk, and visual loss and corneal abrasion are unrelated to the oxygen-cautery combination.

questions.stem: TEE and synchronized cardioversion are examples of what procedural group commonly managed with carefully selected sedation techniques?
options: Ophthalmic procedures
Gastrointestinal procedures
Short cardiovascular procedures
Peripheral nerve procedures
questions.explanation: TEE, cardioversion, and selected cardiac catheterizations are short cardiovascular procedures often done under sedation, but patients may have poor ventricular function, arrhythmias, or valve disease, so drug choice and dosing are tailored. Ophthalmic, GI, and nerve-block procedures are separate procedural groups.

questions.stem: A patient with severe COPD, predicted difficult airway, and esophageal food impaction is scheduled for EGD. Which principle should determine MAC versus a secured airway?
options: Choose MAC, since EGD usually uses sedation
Aspiration, rescue, comorbidity, procedure
Decide by expected procedure duration
Follow the patient's preference alone
questions.explanation: A procedure that is usually done under sedation is appropriate only when the airway, comorbidities, complexity, and stimulation allow it. This patient may need GA with a protected airway.

questions.stem: A percutaneous biopsy carries meaningful hemorrhage risk. How should that risk affect sedation planning?
options: Bleeding risk matters mainly under general anesthesia
Bleeding risk calls for deeper sedation levels
Access, monitoring, and an escalation plan
Bleeding risk by itself mandates an arterial line
questions.explanation: Meaningful hemorrhage risk means sudden hypotension and tachycardia may occur, so planning includes reliable IV access, monitoring that will detect bleeding early, blood availability, and a plan to escalate or convert to general anesthesia. Deeper sedation adds risk rather than protecting the patient, and an arterial line is chosen by overall risk rather than bleeding risk alone.

questions.stem: Why is shoulder-dislocation reduction often well suited to brief deep sedation in an appropriately selected patient?
options: Prolonged immobility for hours of manipulation
Need for the patient to follow commands throughout
Procedure shares the airway with the proceduralist
Brief, intense stimulus with quick recovery needed
questions.explanation: Joint reduction needs a short period of deep analgesia and muscle relaxation for an intense but brief stimulus, after which the pain largely resolves, so a short-acting agent such as propofol or ketamine with quick recovery fits well. Long immobility would favor another plan, and the procedure does not share the airway, which keeps rescue access open.

questions.stem: During beach-chair MAC, the arm-cuff MAP is 70 mmHg and the external auditory meatus is 20 cm above the cuff. What is the approximate MAP at brain level?
options: About 55 mmHg
About 70 mmHg
About 85 mmHg
About 40 mmHg
questions.explanation: Each centimeter of height difference changes pressure by about 0.75 mmHg (1.36 cmH2O per mmHg). A 20 cm difference is about 15 mmHg, so brain-level MAP is about 70 − 15 = 55 mmHg. Using the cuff value unchanged ignores the gradient, adding 15 reverses its direction, and 40 mmHg comes from using 1.5 mmHg per cm.

questions.stem: During shoulder surgery, the patient's head is turned away and draped, and the face is hard to reach. What risk increases if sedation deepens?
options: Higher aspiration risk from head rotation
Venous air embolism from head elevation
Delayed airway rescue if obstruction occurs
Reduced FRC from lateral neck flexion
questions.explanation: With the head turned away and draped for shoulder surgery, the anesthesia provider cannot quickly reach the face to reposition the jaw, insert an airway, or mask ventilate. If sedation deepens and obstruction develops, rescue is delayed. Head rotation does not itself raise aspiration risk, and venous air embolism relates to the beach-chair position.

questions.stem: Which procedural combination most strongly argues against deep sedation with an unsecured airway?
options: Low stimulation with easy airway access
Short duration with a cooperative patient
A procedure that can be stopped immediately
Intense stimulation, poor access, no pause
questions.explanation: Deep sedation with an unsecured airway is hardest to justify when intense, changing stimulation drives repeated dosing, the airway is hard to reach, and the procedure cannot be stopped for rescue. Each distractor removes one of those hazards.

questions.stem: Which THREE factors most determine whether a long interventional radiology case suits sedation? (Select 3)
options: The proceduralist's preferred sedative
Required duration of immobility
Ability to pause the procedure
Availability of a BIS monitor
Planned total contrast volume
Position and airway access
questions.explanation: Sedation suitability depends on whether the team can stop for rescue, how accessible the airway is in the required position, and how long the patient must lie still. Contrast volume matters for kidney protection, a BIS monitor is optional, and the proceduralist's drug preference does not make a case safer.

questions.stem: Late in a prolonged MAC, a previously comfortable patient becomes restless. What should occur before simply escalating sedative doses?
options: Check pain, position, bladder, hypoxemia, block
Treat restlessness as inadequate hypnosis
Give propofol boluses until the patient is still
Add midazolam to blunt the agitation quickly
questions.explanation: Long cases make patients restless, which prompts more drug and raises the chance of deeper-than-intended sedation. Consider whether discomfort, position, or a full bladder is the real cause.

questions.stem: Deep sedation is requested for a prone patient whose airway would be difficult to access. What is the safest planning response?
options: Proceed, since SpO2 will warn early enough
Consider GA with a secured airway instead
Proceed and roll supine if problems arise
Deepen with ketamine, since it spares the airway
questions.explanation: When deep sedation is needed and the airway cannot be reached in the prone position, any obstruction or apnea becomes hard to rescue, so securing the airway before positioning may be safer. Turning a draped prone patient supine takes time, SpO2 warns late on oxygen, and ketamine can still cause laryngospasm, apnea, and secretions.

questions.stem: A laterally positioned patient under MAC develops mild hypoxemia. Which mechanical change can contribute?
options: Higher FRC and compliance in the dependent lung
More perfusion to the nondependent upper lung
Lower FRC and compliance in the dependent lung
Less perfusion to the dependent lower lung
questions.explanation: In the lateral position the abdominal contents and mediastinum compress the dependent lung, lowering its FRC and compliance and promoting atelectasis, while gravity still sends most perfusion there, so V/Q mismatch causes mild hypoxemia. Gravity sends less, not more, perfusion to the nondependent lung, and the dependent lung keeps the larger share of blood flow.

questions.stem: After an 8-hour prone spine fusion with 3 L blood loss, a patient reports painless loss of vision in both eyes. The early fundus exam is normal. What is the most likely cause?
options: Central retinal artery occlusion
Corneal abrasion from exposure
Cortical blindness from embolic stroke
Posterior ischemic optic neuropathy
questions.explanation: Painless bilateral vision loss after long prone spine surgery with large blood loss and a normal early fundus is the classic picture of posterior ischemic optic neuropathy, the most common cause of postoperative visual loss in this setting. Central retinal artery occlusion follows direct globe pressure and is usually unilateral with a cherry-red spot, and a corneal abrasion is painful.

questions.stem: Which common procedure most often pairs a very brief but intense stimulus with a need for rapid recovery?
options: Electrical cardioversion
Routine colonoscopy
Diagnostic TEE
Cataract extraction under topical
questions.explanation: Cardioversion delivers a brief but very painful shock, so it needs deep sedation or general anesthesia for a few seconds and then quick return to baseline. Colonoscopy and TEE last longer with more moderate, sustained stimulation, and cataract surgery under topical anesthesia needs only light sedation with a cooperative patient.

questions.stem: During deep sedation for colonoscopy, firm abdominal pressure is applied. The patient then coughs, SpO2 falls to 88%, and new right lower lobe crackles and wheezes appear. What is the most likely cause?
options: Bronchospasm from airway irritation by itself
Aspiration of regurgitated gastric contents
Atelectasis from sedation hypoventilation
Negative-pressure pulmonary edema
questions.explanation: Abdominal pressure raises intragastric pressure while deep sedation blunts protective reflexes, and cough with desaturation and new right lower lobe findings fits aspiration, since the right lower lobe is the usual dependent target. Bronchospasm explains wheeze but not focal crackles, and negative-pressure edema needs forceful inspiration against an obstructed airway.

questions.stem: During a burn dressing change under sedation, pain spikes briefly with each layer removed. Which adjunct best adds analgesia while largely preserving respiratory drive?
options: Additional midazolam
Fentanyl bolus
Low-dose ketamine
Dexmedetomidine bolus
questions.explanation: Ketamine gives strong analgesia through NMDA antagonism while largely preserving respiratory drive and airway reflexes, which suits brief, intense pain such as a burn dressing change. Fentanyl treats the pain but adds respiratory depression, midazolam adds no analgesia, and a dexmedetomidine bolus acts too slowly and can cause bradycardia and transient hypertension.

questions.stem: Why can carpal-tunnel release often be performed with effective local anesthesia and only minimal systemic sedation?
options: Tourniquet pain cannot develop with it
Infiltration blocks most nociceptive input
The hand needs no immobility for surgery
Sedatives alone provide most analgesia
questions.explanation: Carpal tunnel release is a small, superficial procedure, so effective local infiltration or a field block removes most nociceptive input and light anxiolysis is enough. Tourniquet discomfort can still develop as time passes, and sedatives such as propofol and midazolam add little analgesia, so relying on them would push depth up instead.

questions.stem: Why does MRI sedation demand special rescue planning even though the scan itself is painless?
options: Scanner noise causes intense stimulation
No incision means monitoring is optional
Remote bore and MRI-safe gear slow rescue
The bore improves access to the airway
questions.explanation: MRI suites are often far from help, the bore limits access to the patient's head, and only MRI-safe monitors and airway equipment can enter the scanner room. Rescue often means stopping the scan and moving the patient out, so the plan and equipment are set before sedation. Scanner noise is unpleasant but not painful.

questions.stem: A supine patient with severe OSA repeatedly obstructs during sedation. Which positional adjustment may improve upper-airway patency if the procedure permits?
options: Flat supine with the neck flexed
Trendelenburg with the head turned
Supine with a tall pillow under the head
Lateral or semi-upright position
questions.explanation: Lateral and semi-upright positions keep the tongue and soft palate from falling against the posterior pharynx and reduce the collapsibility of the OSA airway, often enough to stop repeated obstruction. A tall pillow flexes the neck and narrows the airway, and Trendelenburg adds abdominal pressure against the diaphragm.

questions.stem: During sedated TEE, hypoxemia develops and airway maneuvers are difficult. Which procedural factor contributes directly?
options: Left lateral position raises FRC
The probe occupies the pharynx
Propofol directly increases shunt
Topical lidocaine paralyzes the cords
questions.explanation: During TEE the probe sits in the pharynx and esophagus, so jaw thrust, oral airways, and mask ventilation are hampered until it is withdrawn. Lateral positioning lowers rather than raises dependent-lung FRC, propofol causes hypoventilation rather than a direct shunt, and topical lidocaine blunts reflexes without paralyzing the vocal cords.

questions.stem: A procedure alternates between minimal stimulation and brief intense pain. What is the principal titration challenge?
options: Requirements stay constant across the case
Keep the deepest level needed throughout
Drug effect outlasts pain, causing oversedation
Pain changes analgesia needs but not depth
questions.explanation: Sedatives and opioids given to cover a brief painful peak keep acting after the stimulus ends, and once stimulation drops the same blood level produces a deeper state, so apnea or obstruction often follows the painful step. Holding the deepest level throughout magnifies this. A better plan times short-acting doses or local anesthetic to the painful moments.

questions.stem: During beach-chair MAC, a patient becomes confused with arm BP 92/54 mmHg. Which explanation should be considered urgently?
options: Upright positioning protects cerebral flow
Dependent-lung collapse best explains it
Emergence delirium from propofol
Brain perfusion may be lower than the cuff shows
questions.explanation: In the beach-chair position, pressure at brain level is lower than an arm cuff reading because of the hydrostatic gradient, so new confusion with a BP of 92/54 should prompt urgent evaluation of cerebral perfusion. Delirium and other causes can be considered once perfusion has been addressed.

questions.stem: Why must position be considered during MAC even when no airway device is planned?
options: It changes airway patency, access, and physiology
It matters mainly once the patient is prone
It matters mainly after conversion to GA
It affects surgical exposure but not airway
questions.explanation: Even without an airway device, position changes pharyngeal patency, FRC, venous return, and how fast the provider can reach the airway, and a sedated patient cannot protect against pressure or stretch injuries. Prone is the extreme case but not the only one; lateral, beach-chair, and steep head-down positions each change rescue access or physiology.

questions.stem: A sedated patient breathing spontaneously lies in the lateral decubitus position. How is ventilation distributed compared with paralysis and positive-pressure ventilation?
options: More to the upper lung, as with PPV
More to the dependent lung, matching perfusion
Equal to both lungs in either mode
More to the upper lung, matching perfusion
questions.explanation: During spontaneous breathing the dependent hemidiaphragm is pushed higher and contracts more forcefully, so the dependent lung gets more ventilation, matching its gravity-driven perfusion. With paralysis and positive pressure, the compliant upper lung gets more ventilation while perfusion stays dependent, creating mismatch. Picking the upper lung confuses the two modes.

questions.stem: A patient in steep Trendelenburg for prolonged robotic surgery develops marked facial and conjunctival edema. Which emergence concern should this finding raise most directly?
options: Postoperative visual loss from venous congestion
Corneal edema with blurred vision
Hypovolemia from third spacing
Upper-airway edema and difficult extubation
questions.explanation: Visible facial and conjunctival edema after steep Trendelenburg suggests similar edema in the upper airway, so a cuff-leak test and readiness for difficult reintubation come first at emergence. Visual loss and corneal edema are eye concerns that matter less in the next minutes than an airway that may close after extubation.

questions.stem: Why is it incorrect to treat MAC as a fixed depth between moderate and deep sedation?
options: It describes an anesthesia service, not a depth
MAC is the formal ASA label for deep sedation
MAC excludes patients receiving local or regional
MAC is defined by the use of propofol infusions
questions.explanation: ASA defines MAC as a specific anesthesia service for a diagnostic or therapeutic procedure, and it can range from no sedation to general anesthesia while the provider stays ready to convert. Depth is assessed separately on the sedation continuum. MAC often accompanies local or regional anesthesia, and no particular drug defines it.

questions.stem: During a case planned as MAC, a propofol bolus makes the patient unresponsive to painful stimulation and ventilation requires support. What is the most accurate interpretation?
options: Moderate sedation, since it was booked as MAC
General anesthesia; manage and document it
Deep sedation, since breathing continues
Nurse sedation, since MAC has ended
questions.explanation: MAC describes a planned anesthesia service, not a guaranteed depth. If the patient becomes unarousable even to painful stimulation, the physiologic depth is general anesthesia and must be managed accordingly. Billing/documentation terminology should reflect the actual anesthetic care rather than implying that a MAC label overrides the observed depth.

questions.stem: Why is credentialing for nurse-administered moderate sedation not equivalent to providing MAC?
options: Moderate-sedation credentials also cover GA
The roles are identical without propofol
MAC needs anesthesia-level rescue skills
MAC requires no airway expertise
questions.explanation: MAC is a specific anesthesia service furnished by a qualified anesthesia professional who performs a preanesthetic evaluation, provides intra-procedure anesthesia care, and is prepared to rescue the airway or convert the anesthetic when necessary. Scope and credentialing for non-anesthesia moderate sedation are governed separately.

questions.stem: Which THREE components are part of the MAC anesthesia service? (Select 3)
options: Postprocedure anesthesia management
Nursing documentation of vital signs
Intraprocedure anesthetic care
Performing the surgical procedure
Obtaining surgical consent
Preprocedure evaluation
questions.explanation: MAC is a full anesthesia service that includes preprocedure evaluation, intraprocedure anesthetic care with monitoring and readiness to convert, and postprocedure anesthesia management. The surgeon performs the procedure and obtains surgical consent, and nursing documentation does not substitute for the anesthesia service.

questions.stem: Which medication strategy can be part of MAC when appropriate to the procedure and patient?
options: Paralysis to keep an unsecured patient still
Local anesthetic infiltration without drugs
Benzodiazepines and opioids, but not propofol
A tailored sedative, analgesic, or local mix
questions.explanation: MAC uses a mix of anxiolytic, hypnotic, analgesic, and amnestic drugs tailored to the patient and procedure, often combined with local or regional anesthesia. Propofol is commonly used, so excluding it is wrong. Paralysis without a secured airway is never part of MAC, and local alone with no anesthesia care is not a MAC service.

questions.stem: During MAC, a field block fails; severe pain persists, and attempts to deepen sedation repeatedly cause obstruction. What should the anesthesia provider be prepared to do?
options: Change the plan, including GA with a secured airway
Keep escalating propofol despite the obstruction
Add an opioid bolus and continue the same plan
Give a paralytic to stop movement and continue
questions.explanation: When the block has failed and every attempt to deepen sedation causes obstruction, the technique has failed on two fronts, so the plan should change to surgeon-supplemented local or GA with a secured airway. An opioid bolus adds analgesia but worsens the same respiratory problem, and paralysis without a secured airway is not acceptable.

questions.stem: A facility proposes skipping the airway assessment because a patient is scheduled for MAC rather than general anesthesia. What is the key flaw?
options: Airway exams matter just when intubation is planned
Depth can change, so rescue must be planned
The proceduralist's airway exam is sufficient
MAC rarely progresses past moderate sedation
questions.explanation: MAC carries the same preanesthetic evaluation expectations as general anesthesia because sedation can deepen without warning or the procedure can require conversion, and the rescue plan depends on knowing whether the airway is difficult. A proceduralist's screening does not replace the anesthesia evaluation, and the airway exam matters most when intubation is not planned, since any rescue would be unplanned.

questions.stem: Absolute immobility is required for a procedure despite adequate analgesia. Which capability can general anesthesia provide that routine MAC cannot safely guarantee?
options: Reliable amnesia for the procedure
Effective local anesthetic infiltration
Supplemental oxygen delivery
Neuromuscular blockade with a secured airway
questions.explanation: When absolute immobility is required, general anesthesia can provide it with neuromuscular blockade and a secured airway. MAC can provide amnesia, local anesthesia, and supplemental oxygen, but cannot safely guarantee that the patient will not move. Paralysis without a secured airway is never acceptable.

questions.stem: What fundamentally distinguishes intended moderate sedation from an anesthesia-provider MAC service?
options: MAC is a service set at deep sedation
MAC is a service prepared for any depth
Moderate sedation requires an anesthetist
MAC is a service that excludes regional blocks
questions.explanation: MAC is a service defined by an anesthesia professional who is prepared to manage any depth, including conversion to general anesthesia, whereas intended moderate sedation is a depth that nonanesthesia providers can deliver. MAC is not tied to one depth and can be combined with local or regional anesthesia.

questions.stem: During an otherwise stable MAC, the anesthesia professional leaves the room and the patient becomes apneic. Which principle was violated?
options: Presence required at induction and emergence
Presence required once the case converts to GA
Qualified anesthesia personnel present throughout
Presence required for ASA III and higher patients
questions.explanation: ASA basic standards require qualified anesthesia personnel in the room throughout every general anesthetic, regional anesthetic, and MAC, because depth and physiology can change at any time. A stable course does not relax the rule, and it does not depend on ASA class. Apnea that develops while no one is watching is exactly the event the standard exists to catch.

questions.stem: Which item is NOT routinely required solely because a case is performed under MAC?
options: Airway-rescue capability
Preanesthetic evaluation and plan
Invasive arterial catheterization
Postanesthesia care
questions.explanation: MAC requires a preanesthesia evaluation and plan, continuous monitoring, airway rescue capability, readiness to convert to general anesthesia, and postanesthesia care. An arterial line is chosen for patient or procedural reasons such as severe cardiac disease, not because the case is done under MAC.

questions.stem: Which THREE elements are essential to a safe MAC system? (Select 3)
options: Immediately available airway equipment
Readiness to convert to general anesthesia
Routine arterial line placement
Mandatory volatile-agent maintenance
Consent signed by the proceduralist
A qualified anesthesia professional
questions.explanation: MAC is safe because an anesthesia professional is present who can rescue the airway with equipment at hand and convert to general anesthesia when needed. MAC commonly uses IV agents without volatiles, arterial lines are case-specific, and consent for anesthesia care is obtained by the anesthesia provider rather than only by the proceduralist.

questions.stem: A MAC patient obstructs, but the room has only nasal oxygen and suction. What preparation was inadequate?
options: Nothing; nasal oxygen and suction suffice
Routine intubation at the start of MAC
A code team in place of bedside rescue
Positive-pressure and advanced airway equipment
questions.explanation: MAC requires immediate access to positive-pressure ventilation and advanced airway equipment, such as a bag-mask, oral and nasal airways, SGAs, and a laryngoscope. Nasal oxygen and suction cannot ventilate an obstructed patient, and waiting for a code team delays rescue. Routine intubation at the start would defeat the purpose of MAC.

questions.stem: After MAC, a drowsy patient is sent toward discharge without monitored recovery or reassessment. What is missing?
options: Ongoing assessment, monitoring, and records
A successful ambulation test before discharge
A final blood pressure taken at the bedside
Confirmation that the patient can speak clearly
questions.explanation: ASA postanesthesia standards apply after MAC, so the patient needs monitored recovery, reassessment by qualified staff, and documentation until discharge criteria are met. Drowsiness after sedation can progress to hypoventilation once stimulation stops. Speaking, walking, or one normal blood pressure are parts of a discharge assessment, not substitutes for monitored recovery.

questions.stem: A MAC preoperative note lists NPO status and allergies but omits severe OSA, GERD, medications, and prior difficult intubation. Which deficiency is most important?
options: A routine chest radiograph is missing
Airway, aspiration, and comorbidity risks
A routine stress test is missing
The surgeon's sedative preference is missing
questions.explanation: Severe OSA, GERD, current medications, and a prior difficult intubation define the airway, aspiration, and comorbidity risks that shape a MAC plan and the conversion plan. Missing them is the critical deficiency. A routine chest radiograph or stress test is not required without specific indications, and the surgeon's preference does not replace the assessment.

questions.stem: A continuous propofol technique is planned, but no reliable infusion pump is available. What is the best response?
options: Estimate the rate by counting drops
Run the propofol by gravity
Get a pump or change to a deliverable plan
Proceed; dose precision is unneeded in MAC
questions.explanation: A continuous propofol technique needs a reliable infusion pump, because drop counting and gravity delivery cannot give accurate or steady doses and risk oversedation or awareness. Without a pump, the plan changes to one that can be delivered safely, such as intermittent boluses. Dose precision matters as much in MAC as in GA.

questions.stem: Why does a remote procedure room with imaging equipment blocking the head increase MAC risk?
options: Imaging gear raises the patient's sedative needs
Remote rooms lessen the need for rescue gear
Radiation exposure limits provider time at the bedside
Blocked access delays airway rescue and conversion
questions.explanation: When imaging equipment surrounds the head, jaw thrust, mask ventilation, and intubation all take longer to start, and remote sites often have fewer helpers and less familiar equipment. Planning means confirming access, rescue gear, and help before sedating. Radiation safety does limit time near the table, but it does not explain the airway risk.

questions.stem: A high-risk TAVR is planned under MAC. Why must the person providing the anesthetic have advanced airway and general-anesthesia rescue capability?
options: MAC can deepen or need rapid conversion to GA
Propofol use mandates tracheal intubation
Moderate sedation training matches MAC training
Rapid pacing requires a secured airway
questions.explanation: MAC is defined by an anesthesia provider who can rescue the airway and convert to general anesthesia, and TAVR adds risks such as annular rupture and sudden hemodynamic collapse that may require immediate intubation. Propofol does not mandate intubation, rapid pacing is routinely done under MAC, and moderate sedation credentials do not cover general anesthesia rescue.

questions.stem: A sedated patient opens the eyes and says their name only after a firm trapezius squeeze. RR is 8, and jaw thrust is needed intermittently. Which ASA level fits?
options: Moderate sedation/analgesia
Deep sedation/analgesia
Minimal sedation (anxiolysis)
General anesthesia
questions.explanation: A purposeful response to repeated or painful stimulation, an intermittent need for airway support, and possibly inadequate ventilation define deep sedation. Moderate sedation requires a purposeful response to voice or light touch with no airway intervention, and general anesthesia means no arousal even to pain. Saying a name is purposeful, unlike reflex withdrawal.

questions.stem: Which scenario most clearly represents MAC?
options: A patient self-administers oral anxiolysis
A nurse gives protocolized moderate sedation
An anesthetist manages it with rescue readiness
A proceduralist sedates while operating
questions.explanation: MAC is a service provided by a qualified anesthesia professional who monitors the patient, manages sedation, and is ready to rescue the airway or convert to general anesthesia. Protocolized nurse sedation and proceduralist-directed sedation are moderate sedation services, and self-administered oral anxiolysis is not an anesthesia service.

questions.stem: During MAC, coughing, agitation, and movement make the procedure unsafe despite attempts to correct reversible causes. What should the anesthesia professional be prepared to do?
options: Finish the procedure before changing the plan
Keep escalating sedation until movement stops
Let the surgeon decide whether rescue is needed
Change the plan, including conversion to GA
questions.explanation: When coughing, agitation, and movement persist after reversible causes such as hypoxemia, pain, and a full bladder are addressed, the technique no longer allows a safe procedure, and the anesthesia professional must be ready to convert to general anesthesia. Escalating sedation without a secured airway trades movement for obstruction and apnea, and the anesthesia decision belongs to the anesthesia provider.

questions.stem: A remote endoscopy room lacks capnography, positive-pressure ventilation equipment, and emergency drugs. Which THREE deficiencies must be corrected before anesthesia-provider MAC? (Select 3)
options: Processed EEG monitoring
Emergency medications
An arterial line setup
Ventilation monitoring
A volatile anesthetic vaporizer
Positive-pressure ventilation capability
questions.explanation: Anesthesia-provider MAC requires capnography for ventilation monitoring, a way to deliver positive-pressure ventilation, and emergency drugs, along with oxygen, suction, and airway equipment. Processed EEG, an arterial line, and a vaporizer may help in some cases but are not missing minimum requirements.

questions.stem: During cataract MAC, a patient briefly stops responding to voice after propofol but still responds purposefully to repeated tactile stimulation and ventilates adequately. What is the best interpretation?
options: Deep sedation, now managed at that depth
General anesthesia, since voice response is lost
Moderate sedation, since touch gets a response
Minimal sedation with a brief drug peak
questions.explanation: Losing response to voice but responding purposefully to repeated touch places the patient in deep sedation, where airway support may be needed even though ventilation is adequate now. Moderate sedation requires a response to voice or light touch, and general anesthesia means no purposeful response to any stimulus. The MAC label does not change the depth assessment.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for MAC drank coffee with whole milk 3 hours ago. How should ASA fasting guidance apply?
options: Proceed, since clear liquids need 2 hours
Proceed, since MAC has no fasting rule
Delay until 6 hours after the milk
Delay until 8 hours after the milk
questions.explanation: ASA fasting guidance applies to MAC and sedation as it does to general anesthesia, because airway reflexes can be depressed. Coffee with whole milk is not a clear liquid; nonhuman milk is treated like a light meal, with a 6-hour fast. The 8-hour interval is for fried or fatty foods and meat.

questions.stem: Monitors and sedatives are ready for MAC, but no airway device, induction medications, or conversion strategy has been prepared. What is missing?
options: An executable intubation or LMA rescue plan
A postoperative opioid prescription plan
A plan for routine neuromuscular blockade
A discharge and escort plan
questions.explanation: MAC preparation is not complete until airway devices, induction drugs, suction, and a defined conversion strategy are ready, because the case can need general anesthesia without warning. Postoperative analgesia and discharge planning matter but do not help in the minute after obstruction or failed sedation, and routine neuromuscular blockade has no role in MAC.

questions.stem: Which THREE patient factors most increase risk during MAC? (Select 3)
options: Well-controlled hypothyroidism
Age 35 with BMI 29 kg/m²
Chronic high-dose opioid use
Pulmonary hypertension
Mild intermittent asthma
Severe obstructive sleep apnea
questions.explanation: Pulmonary hypertension leaves the right ventricle vulnerable to hypoxemia and hypercarbia, severe OSA makes obstruction likely under sedation, and chronic opioid use makes drug requirements and respiratory responses unpredictable. Controlled hypothyroidism, mild asthma without recent symptoms, and a young overweight patient carry far less sedation risk.

questions.stem: Why does inability to tolerate the required position or duration increase risk during MAC?
options: It mainly raises the risk of postoperative nausea
Restlessness drives deeper sedation and airway risk
It affects surgical exposure but not airway safety
It mainly raises pressure-injury risk at bony points
questions.explanation: A patient who cannot lie still for the required time or position becomes restless, which pushes the team to give more sedative with an unprotected airway, and that escalation is where obstruction and apnea occur. That may favor GA from the start. Pressure injury is a real positioning risk, but it is not the main reason intolerance raises MAC risk.

questions.stem: Which setup most compromises emergency airway access during MAC?
options: Supine with the face clear of all drapes
Semi-upright with direct access to the head
Prone with the head turned and partly covered
Lateral with the face fully visible to staff
questions.explanation: Prone positioning with the head turned away and draped makes jaw thrust, mask ventilation, and intubation slow to start, so the plan must account for lost access before sedating. Lateral and semi-upright positions keep the face reachable and can even improve airway patency compared with supine.

questions.stem: A regional block is combined with titrated propofol sedation managed by an anesthesia professional with full rescue capability. How is the anesthesia service best described?
options: Regional anesthesia only because a block was placed
MAC combined with regional anesthesia
General anesthesia solely because propofol was used
Moderate sedation solely because the patient remained arousable
questions.explanation: When an anesthesia professional places or supports a regional block and adds titrated propofol sedation with full rescue capability, the service is MAC combined with regional anesthesia. Propofol use does not make it general anesthesia, and arousability does not make it moderate sedation, because MAC is defined by the anesthesia service.

questions.stem: After 20 minutes of propofol MAC for cataract surgery, the patient is awake and oriented, SpO2 is 97% on room air, vital signs are stable, and pain is minimal. Which disposition fits?
options: Mandatory Phase I PACU stay after any MAC
Immediate discharge home from the procedure room
Hold in Phase I until 60 minutes have passed
Fast-track directly to Phase II recovery
questions.explanation: Patients who meet fast-track criteria in the procedure room, such as being awake and oriented with stable vital signs, adequate oxygenation on room air, and controlled pain and nausea, can bypass Phase I and go to Phase II recovery. MAC does not mandate a Phase I stay, but discharge straight home skips the postanesthesia assessment that is still required.

questions.stem: A procedural sedation nurse and a CRNA use similar drugs. What most clearly distinguishes the CRNA's MAC service?
options: Anesthesia-level rescue and conversion
Reaching deep sedation in every case
Using propofol rather than midazolam
Using local anesthetic infiltration
questions.explanation: The CRNA's MAC service is defined by anesthesia-level assessment, airway rescue, and the ability to convert to general anesthesia, not by the drug used or the depth reached. A sedation nurse may give similar drugs under protocol. MAC does not require deep sedation in each case, and local infiltration is often done by the surgeon.

questions.stem: During MAC for a facial procedure, the surgical field covers the nose and mouth so exhaled CO2 cannot be sampled. What does the ASA ventilation standard require?
options: Cancel the case until CO2 can be sampled
Use SpO2 trends as the ventilation monitor
Clinical signs, documenting why CO2 is precluded
Intubate, since capnography is mandatory
questions.explanation: ASA basic standards call for exhaled CO2 monitoring during moderate or deep sedation unless it is precluded or invalidated by the patient, procedure, or equipment. When that happens, ventilation is still assessed by continual clinical signs and the reason is documented. SpO2 tracks oxygenation, not ventilation, so it cannot replace that assessment.

questions.stem: Why does a healthy patient still require a meaningful anesthesia preoperative evaluation before MAC?
options: MAC removes airway risk in healthy patients
ASA III–IV patients need the evaluation most
A brief note suffices for short procedures
Depth can change, so all usual risks still matter
questions.explanation: MAC can drift into deep sedation or general anesthesia at any moment, so even a healthy patient needs the same airway, aspiration, medication, and comorbidity review as for general anesthesia. MAC does not remove airway risk, and a brief note is not enough for a short case.

questions.stem: During MAC, a patient stops responding even to painful stimulation for several minutes but keeps breathing spontaneously without an airway device. Which statement is accurate?
options: This is general anesthesia
This is deep sedation
This is moderate sedation
This is MAC; depth is not classified
questions.explanation: ASA defines general anesthesia by unarousable loss of consciousness, even to painful stimulation, whether or not an airway device is used or the patient breathes spontaneously. Spontaneous ventilation is the tempting reason to call it deep sedation, but deep sedation still requires a purposeful response to repeated or painful stimulation. The MAC label does not replace classifying the actual depth.

questions.stem: In closed claims analyses of MAC, which mechanism most often caused death or permanent brain injury?
options: Operating room fires during head cases
Respiratory depression from oversedation
Medication errors from syringe swaps
Cardiovascular events from hypotension
questions.explanation: Closed claims analyses of MAC found that respiratory depression from absolute or relative sedative overdose was the leading mechanism of death and permanent brain injury, and many events were judged preventable with better monitoring such as capnography and closer vigilance. OR fires were a notable MAC-specific injury in head and neck cases with open oxygen, but they were less common than respiratory events.

questions.stem: After MAC with midazolam and fentanyl, a patient meets discharge criteria and plans to drive home alone. What is appropriate?
options: Allow driving after a 2-hour PACU observation
Discharge alone by taxi once criteria are met
Discharge with a responsible adult to accompany
Allow driving once alert and oriented x4
questions.explanation: Residual sedative effects on judgment and reaction time outlast the point at which a patient looks alert, so after sedation the patient should go home with a responsible adult and should not drive that day. Meeting discharge criteria or waiting longer in PACU does not clear psychomotor impairment, and a taxi ride alone leaves no one to watch for delayed sedation or falls.

questions.stem: Adequate local anesthesia controls pain, but the patient is anxious about recalling the procedure. Which drug property may be useful as part of a balanced MAC technique?
options: Analgesia
Anxiolysis
Immobility
Amnesia
questions.explanation: The patient's pain is already controlled; the concern is remembering the procedure, which amnestic drugs such as midazolam address. Anxiolysis is a close second, since the patient is anxious, but it targets the worry rather than the recall. Analgesia is already provided, and immobility is not the goal.

questions.stem: Midazolam and fentanyl are titrated together for moderate sedation. What is the principal safety implication of this multimodal strategy?
options: Better comfort, but synergistic respiratory depression
Two agents guarantee lighter sedation
The combination prevents respiratory depression
Fentanyl prevents benzodiazepine obstruction
questions.explanation: Midazolam supplies anxiolysis, sedation, and amnesia while fentanyl supplies analgesia, so the combination can improve procedural tolerance. Both also depress ventilation, and together they can produce synergistic respiratory depression that is greater than expected from either dose alone.

questions.stem: A remote interventional-radiology suite lacks backup suction and capnography. What principle applies?
options: Remote sites may drop respiratory monitoring
Remote sites need the same rescue standards
SpO2 can substitute for capnography off-site
Suction is needed just for GA cases off-site
questions.explanation: Anesthesia care in a remote location should provide monitoring, oxygenation and ventilation support, suction, emergency drugs, and rescue resources appropriate to the patient and anesthetic. Safety expectations do not drop because the procedure is outside the main OR, and SpO2 cannot stand in for capnography when supplemental oxygen is given.

questions.stem: Which THREE issues matter most before prolonged shoulder MAC in a frail patient with COPD and kyphosis? (Select 3)
options: Airway access under drapes
Planned neuromuscular blockade
Routine arterial line placement
A plan for conversion to GA
Tolerance of the required position
A predetermined BIS target
questions.explanation: Kyphosis and COPD make the beach-chair position and a long duration hard to tolerate, drapes limit airway access if obstruction develops, and a conversion plan is needed because any of these can fail mid-case. A BIS target and an arterial line are not standard requirements for MAC, and neuromuscular blockade would require a secured airway.

questions.stem: A patient with severe cardiovascular disease is scheduled for MAC. Which planning priority is most important?
options: Use lighter sedation so instability can't occur
Limit monitoring to reduce stimulation
Plan for low reserve: monitors, drugs, conversion
Plan an inhaled induction regardless
questions.explanation: Severe cardiovascular disease means little reserve to tolerate hypotension, tachycardia, or hypoxemia, so the plan includes appropriate monitoring, vasoactive drugs ready, careful titration, and a conversion plan. Lighter sedation lowers but does not remove the risk, and reducing monitoring hides instability.

questions.stem: During MAC, the patient becomes unresponsive to painful stimulation and ventilation becomes inadequate. What is the correct response?
options: Continue unchanged, since the case is MAC
Reclassify the patient as moderately sedated
Wait for spontaneous recovery
Treat as GA: support ventilation, escalate plan
questions.explanation: Unresponsiveness to painful stimulation with inadequate ventilation is general anesthesia, whatever the case was booked as. The provider supports ventilation, reduces or stops the sedative, and moves to the conversion plan if needed. Continuing unchanged or waiting for spontaneous recovery risks hypoxemia.

questions.stem: Which provider capability is essential for high-risk MAC such as TAVR?
options: An anesthetist able to rescue and convert
ACLS certification without anesthesia training
Moderate-sedation credentialing
Skill in administering propofol
questions.explanation: High-risk MAC cases such as TAVR need an anesthesia professional who can manage hemodynamic collapse, rescue the airway, and convert to general anesthesia at once. ACLS certification, moderate sedation credentialing, or skill with propofol alone do not provide that level of airway and anesthetic management.

questions.stem: Which statement about MAC and moderate sedation is incorrect?
options: Intended moderate sedation preserves purposeful responsiveness
MAC is an anesthesia service
MAC may encompass changing depths
They are identical services distinguished only by the drug chosen
questions.explanation: MAC and moderate sedation are different services. Moderate sedation keeps purposeful response and can be given by trained nonanesthesia providers, while MAC is an anesthesia service that may cover changing depths with readiness to convert to general anesthesia. The drug chosen does not define either service, so that statement is the incorrect one.

questions.stem: Which developments commonly force conversion from MAC to general anesthesia?
options: Mild anxiety, brief nausea, or one low BP
Snoring relieved by a chin lift
Failed block, intolerance, or airway failure
Transient hypertension at incision
questions.explanation: Large case series show that failed regional or neuraxial anesthesia, patient intolerance of MAC, and hypoxemia or airway failure are the usual reasons for converting to general anesthesia. Snoring that resolves with a chin lift and brief hypertension at incision are expected, correctable events that call for adjustment rather than a change of technique.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which THREE changes during MAC should prompt serious consideration of conversion/escalation? (Select 3)
options: Persistent severe hypercapnia despite initial airway/ventilation maneuvers
Loss of reliable IV access when IV anesthesia/rescue drugs are required
A procedural change that substantially increases invasiveness/stimulation
Mild anxiety relieved by reassurance
Stable physiology with adequate comfort
A brief isolated BP decrease corrected immediately
questions.explanation: Persistent hypercapnia despite airway maneuvers, loss of reliable IV access when IV drugs are needed, and a procedural change that greatly increases stimulation are strong reasons to escalate or convert. Mild anxiety eased by reassurance, stable physiology, and a brief blood pressure dip that corrects promptly are managed within MAC.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During propofol MAC for EGD, as the scope passes, the patient makes high-pitched inspiratory noises, then strong chest efforts with no capnogram while SpO2 falls. What is the best response?
options: Bronchospasm; withdraw scope, give albuterol
Laryngospasm; withdraw scope, CPAP with 100% O2
Aspiration; suction and tilt the head down
Central apnea; give naloxone and observe
questions.explanation: Stridor followed by vigorous effort with no exhaled CO2 means the glottis has closed, which is laryngospasm triggered by the scope or secretions. Treatment is removing the stimulus and applying CPAP with 100% oxygen, deepening or giving succinylcholine if it persists. Bronchospasm causes wheeze and a sloped capnogram rather than silent effort, and central apnea has no chest effort.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient moves during a critical neural portion of surgery despite an otherwise adequate MAC plan. When is conversion appropriate?
options: Whenever voice response is lost
After SpO2 stays below 90% for 30 seconds
When conditions prevent safe continuation
After the scheduled end time passes
