questions.explanation: Conversion to general anesthesia is indicated when conditions prevent safe continuation, such as movement during a critical neural step that sedation cannot control. Loss of voice response, a brief desaturation, or passing the scheduled end time are signals to reassess, but none is an automatic trigger for conversion.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During propofol MAC, the patient becomes agitated, processed-EEG values rise, and the IV site is swollen and cool. What is the best immediate interpretation?
options: Opioid overdose causing agitation
Propofol concentration is too dilute
Paradoxical excitation from propofol
IV infiltration; delivery is unreliable
questions.explanation: A swollen, cool IV site plus loss of expected hypnotic effect suggests infiltration and unreliable intravenous delivery. Giving larger doses through the same catheter can worsen tissue exposure without restoring anesthesia, so new reliable access and an appropriate rescue or conversion plan are needed.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A CRNA hands off an ongoing MAC case for a break. Which handoff content most protects the patient in the next few minutes?
options: Current depth, drugs given, and the airway plan
Surgical progress and expected finish time
Allergy list and preop medication history
Planned postoperative pain prescriptions
questions.explanation: During MAC the next provider most needs to know how deep the patient is, what was given and when, how the airway has behaved, and what the rescue and conversion plan is, since depth can change soon after the handoff. Allergies and surgical progress matter but do not tell the new provider what may go wrong in the next few minutes.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Before MAC, what expectation about consciousness and recall should be discussed?
options: Guaranteed unconsciousness and full amnesia
Possible awareness and recall of some events
No discomfort at any point during the case
Recall only if conversion to GA is needed
questions.explanation: MAC often keeps patients responsive, and amnesia from midazolam or propofol is dose dependent, so patients should hear that they may be awake at times and remember parts of the procedure. Promising full sleep or no discomfort sets up a sense of failure when recall occurs, and recall does not require conversion to GA.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: After MAC, a patient complains, "I was supposed to be completely asleep." Which preoperative intervention most directly reduces this mismatch?
options: Promise deeper sedation if anxiety develops
Give enough midazolam to guarantee amnesia
Explain likely recall and possible conversion
Avoid discussing depth so as not to worry them
questions.explanation: Dissatisfaction after MAC usually comes from a gap between what the patient expected and what was planned, so the fix is an honest preoperative description of the experience, including possible recall and conversion. No midazolam dose guarantees amnesia, and promising deeper sedation on request recreates the same mismatch.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Why is it reasonable to mention possible sore throat even when MAC is planned?
options: Dry nasal oxygen irritates the pharynx for days
Propofol causes chemical pharyngitis on injection
Capnography tubing passes into the hypopharynx
Unexpected conversion may require an airway device
questions.explanation: If MAC converts to general anesthesia, an LMA or endotracheal tube may be placed, and sore throat is a common result, so mentioning it beforehand prevents surprise. Dry oxygen can cause mild dryness but not days of pharyngeal pain, and capnography sampling stays at the nares or mouth.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which TWO expectations are appropriate to discuss before MAC? (Select 2)
options: Recovery-room monitoring will be skipped
The patient may need to follow instructions
They will have no memory of the procedure
They will be fully asleep throughout
Monitoring will be lighter than under GA
Brief discomfort or awareness may occur
questions.explanation: Before MAC, patients should know they may feel brief discomfort or be aware at times and may be asked to follow instructions, and that conversion to general anesthesia is possible. MAC does not promise unconsciousness or amnesia, monitoring standards equal those of general anesthesia, and recovery monitoring still applies.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During orthopedic MAC, a patient may intermittently hear conversation or procedural sounds. How should this be framed beforehand?
options: Hearing sounds can be normal under MAC
Any recall means awareness under GA
Orthopedic MAC should prevent recall
Hearing sounds means the block failed
questions.explanation: Under MAC, patients may drift in and out and hear conversation or procedural sounds, which is expected rather than a sign of awareness under general anesthesia. Setting this expectation before surgery reduces distress and complaints afterward. Hearing sounds does not mean the block has failed.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During MAC, the patient obstructs and SpO2 falls to 84%. What is the immediate priority?
options: Deepen propofol to stop the patient moving
Open the airway and support ventilation
Let the proceduralist finish, then intervene
Raise oxygen flow and watch the SpO2 trend
questions.explanation: Desaturation from obstruction is fixed by relieving the obstruction with jaw thrust, chin lift, or an airway adjunct and assisting ventilation with bag-mask if needed. More oxygen cannot reach alveoli through a closed airway, deeper propofol worsens the obstruction, and the procedure should pause until oxygenation is restored.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient becomes agitated and moves during a critical portion of MAC. What is the best next step?
options: Ignore the movement if SpO2 is normal
Give a large propofol bolus right away
Check reversible causes; convert if unsafe
Paralyze without securing the airway
questions.explanation: Sudden agitation during MAC may come from hypoxemia, hypercarbia, pain from an inadequate block, a full bladder, or disinhibition from sedatives, so reversible causes are checked first. If the procedure still cannot continue safely, conversion to general anesthesia follows. A large propofol bolus risks apnea, and paralysis without a secured airway is dangerous.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During emergency conversion from MAC, the video laryngoscope has no power and induction medications were never prepared. Which planning failure occurred?
options: Rescue gear can be fetched after deterioration
Conversion gear is needed at deep sedation
A conversion plan is for ASA IV patients
Conversion supplies weren't ready before starting
questions.explanation: A conversion-to-GA plan means the video laryngoscope is charged, induction and emergency drugs are drawn up, and the team knows the steps before the first sedative dose. Fetching or checking equipment after deterioration wastes the time needed for rescue. This readiness applies to every MAC case, not only to ASA IV patients.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During EGD under MAC, vomiting occurs with suspected pulmonary aspiration and worsening oxygenation. What should this trigger?
options: Airway management and consideration of conversion
Continue MAC; aspiration doesn't affect the airway
More sedation to suppress coughing
Delay intervention until a chest film
questions.explanation: Aspiration during MAC can rapidly produce airway contamination, hypoxemia, and impaired ventilation. Immediate priorities are suction and restoration of oxygenation and ventilation, with conversion to a secured airway/general anesthesia when needed to protect the lungs and permit safe continuation.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During MAC, which finding most strongly supports escalation or conversion to general anesthesia?
options: SpO2 94% on 2 L with a regular capnogram
ETCO2 65 despite jaw thrust and nasal airway
Heart rate rising from 72 to 86 at incision
Anxiety and fidgeting before the incision
questions.explanation: Persistent hypercapnia after airway repositioning and an adjunct shows that ventilation remains inadequate under the current technique, which calls for assisted ventilation and conversion if it cannot be corrected. An SpO2 of 94% with a regular waveform, a modest heart-rate rise at incision, and preincision anxiety are expected findings managed within MAC.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A diagnostic laparoscopy unexpectedly becomes an open abdominal exploration. Why should the anesthetic plan be reassessed?
options: Opening the abdomen lowers anesthetic requirements
Open surgery removes the aspiration risk of pneumoperitoneum
Stimulation, duration, and airway needs now exceed MAC
MAC must continue once the case has started
questions.explanation: Conversion from laparoscopy to open exploration changes the expected intensity and duration of surgical stimulation and may increase requirements for analgesia, immobility, ventilation control, and airway protection. The anesthetic should therefore be reassessed rather than assuming the original MAC plan remains appropriate.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: After additional midazolam during MAC, a patient becomes more restless and disinhibited while ventilation begins to worsen. What is the best response?
options: Give larger midazolam doses until the patient is calm
Assume the block failed and add more local anesthetic
Add a paralytic to stop movement and keep going
Suspect paradoxical effect; reassess airway first
questions.explanation: Restlessness after additional midazolam can reflect paradoxical disinhibition, excessive sedation with hypoxemia or hypercapnia, pain, or another cause. Worsening ventilation makes reflexively giving more benzodiazepine unsafe, so airway and ventilation are reassessed first while the drug contribution and other causes are evaluated.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which THREE developments commonly lead to conversion from MAC to general anesthesia? (Select 3)
options: Transient SpO2 dip fixed by jaw thrust
Mild hypertension treated with labetalol
Brief anxiety before the incision
Inability to tolerate the procedure under MAC
Hypoxemia or airway obstruction
Failed regional/neuraxial technique
questions.explanation: Common reasons for converting from MAC include failure of the primary regional or neuraxial technique, the patient's inability to tolerate the procedure, and hypoxemia or airway obstruction. A brief desaturation that corrects with jaw thrust, preincision anxiety, and treatable hypertension are managed within MAC.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A spinal anesthetic is inadequate during hip surgery and escalating sedation would be required to tolerate surgical pain. What is the safest next step?
options: Convert to a technique that gives surgical anesthesia
Keep escalating propofol until movement stops
Treat the surgical pain with repeated midazolam
Give a paralytic and continue without an airway
questions.explanation: When a spinal does not cover the surgical stimulus, sedation alone cannot fix it without reaching unsafe depth, so the anesthetic should change, by converting to GA or another reliable technique. Midazolam provides no analgesia, and escalating propofol to suppress movement under pain leads to obstruction and apnea with an unprotected airway.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient anxious about remembering the nerve block asks for midazolam once the block is finished. What should they expect about memory of the block?
options: Erased, since midazolam causes retrograde amnesia
Likely recalled, since amnesia is anterograde
Erased if a larger dose is given soon after
Erased once the infusion reaches steady state
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines produce anterograde amnesia, so they impair memory formation for events after the dose but do not erase memories already formed. Giving midazolam after the block will not remove recall of it, no matter how large the dose. To reduce recall of a stimulus, the drug must be at peak effect before the stimulus.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Two otherwise similar MAC patients receive different counseling: one is told partial awareness/recall may occur; the other is promised complete sleep. Which factor most increases the second patient's risk of dissatisfaction afterward?
options: Expectations alter whether recall occurs
Counseling itself makes recall more likely
Expectation mismatch if recall occurs
The first patient will necessarily receive less sedative
questions.explanation: Recall can occur during MAC because the intended depth may permit responsiveness and amnesia is dose dependent. Dissatisfaction comes from the gap between a promise of complete sleep and what the patient remembers. Expectations and counseling do not change the pharmacology of amnesia, so they do not alter whether recall happens.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During MAC, a patient becomes acutely confused, combative, and unable to cooperate. What is the best next step?
options: Give a large propofol bolus, then assess breathing
Continue unchanged while SpO2 remains normal
Treat it as light sedation and deepen the infusion
Look for hypoxemia, hypercapnia, pain, or drug effect
questions.explanation: Acute confusion and agitation during sedation is often a sign of hypoxemia, hypercapnia, pain, a full bladder, or a paradoxical drug effect, so the cause must be found before giving more sedative. Deepening sedation in an unrecognized hypercapnic or hypoxic patient makes the problem worse, and if the cause cannot be corrected safely, conversion is the next step.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During MAC, severe hypotension and bradycardia persist despite appropriate initial treatment. What should be considered?
options: Give more fluid and continue the MAC
Escalate resuscitation; consider converting
Deepen propofol to blunt the stress response
Repeat the initial drugs and keep observing
questions.explanation: Severe hypotension and bradycardia that persist after appropriate first-line treatment mean the problem has outgrown the MAC setup, so resuscitation escalates with vasopressors, chronotropes, and airway support, and conversion to general anesthesia is considered. Repeating what already failed or adding fluid while continuing delays definitive care, and more propofol worsens vasodilation and bradycardia.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Why should a patient be told before MAC that they may need to follow commands?
options: Following commands prevents airway obstruction
Responses can replace physiologic monitoring
MAC requires the patient to remain fully awake
Some cases require cooperation or neuro checks
questions.explanation: MAC often preserves enough responsiveness for purposeful interaction, and some procedures need the patient to help with positioning, hold still on request, report symptoms, or take part in neurologic assessment. Explaining this beforehand prevents surprise. Responsiveness does not replace monitoring, and MAC does not require the patient to stay fully awake.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: MAC for EGD must be converted to general anesthesia because of active upper GI bleeding with blood pooling in the oropharynx. Which airway approach is best?
options: RSI with a cuffed endotracheal tube
Second-generation LMA after propofol
Deeper sedation with a nasal airway
Mask ventilation until the scope is out
questions.explanation: Active upper GI bleeding with blood in the oropharynx is a full-stomach situation, so conversion should use rapid sequence induction and a cuffed tube that protects the trachea. A second-generation LMA offers some gastric drainage but does not reliably prevent aspiration of blood, and mask ventilation or deeper sedation leaves the airway unprotected.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which preoperative statement most clearly requires correction before MAC?
options: "You'll keep watching my breathing the whole time."
"I'll definitely be out and remember nothing."
"I may hear some sounds and voices in the room."
"I might be asked to follow some instructions."
questions.explanation: MAC is an anesthesia service that may involve minimal through deep sedation, and neither complete unconsciousness nor amnesia is guaranteed. This statement signals a mismatch between the patient's expectation and the planned technique that should be corrected during informed discussion. The other statements are accurate expectations for MAC.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: When MAC unexpectedly requires conversion to general anesthesia, which resource must already be immediately accessible?
options: A reserved ICU bed for postoperative care
A second proceduralist scrubbed in
Advanced airway and ventilation equipment
A neuromonitoring team on standby
questions.explanation: Conversion can be needed within a minute, so induction drugs, working suction, positive-pressure ventilation, and airway devices from LMA to laryngoscope must be at hand before MAC starts. An ICU bed may be needed later for some patients, but it does nothing for the airway at the moment of conversion.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Which event during MAC is least likely, by itself, to justify conversion to general anesthesia?
options: Persistent coughing that prevents safe surgery
Mild anxiety relieved by reassurance
Suspected aspiration with respiratory compromise
Refractory hemodynamic instability
questions.explanation: Mild anxiety that resolves with reassurance does not represent failure of ventilation, airway protection, hemodynamic stability, analgesia, or procedural tolerance. Conversion is more strongly supported when the current technique can no longer safely meet those requirements.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Late in MAC, a patient repeatedly reaches toward the sterile field. What should happen before simply increasing sedation?
options: Give a neuromuscular blocker to stop the reaching
Give propofol boluses until the movement stops
Restrain the arms and continue if BP is normal
Look for pain, hypoxia, hypercapnia, or a full bladder
questions.explanation: Restlessness late in a case often signals pain, hypoxemia, hypercapnia, positioning discomfort, or a full bladder, and more sedative given before those are checked risks deeper sedation in a patient who may already be hypoventilating. If no correctable cause is found and MAC can no longer be done safely, conversion is the next step.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A patient asks whether propofol MAC guarantees no memory. What is the most accurate response?
options: Recall varies; parts may be remembered
Recall shows the patient was never sedated
Amnesia is assured at any sedating dose
Propofol has no effect on memory
questions.explanation: Propofol can produce amnesia, but recall during MAC varies with dose, achieved depth, adjunct medications, and individual response. Because MAC does not require continuous unconsciousness, the patient should be told that portions of the procedure may be remembered.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: A planned 1-hour MAC extends to 3 hours; the patient becomes restless, requires increasing propofol, and begins obstructing. What is the best interpretation?
options: More propofol is the appropriate response
The MAC plan is failing as depth needs rise
An infiltrated IV is the most likely cause
Longer duration lowers the airway risk
questions.explanation: Increasing duration can produce discomfort and fatigue, but the key danger here is the escalating propofol requirement accompanied by recurrent obstruction. That combination shows that maintaining procedural tolerance now requires a depth at which the unsecured airway is no longer reliably safe.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During MAC, RR is 6/min and ETCO2 stays at 62 mmHg despite stimulation and jaw thrust; SpO2 is 95% on oxygen. What is the best next step?
options: Increase oxygen flow and recheck the gas trend
Give naloxone and resume the same propofol rate
Assist breaths with bag-mask and cut sedation
Proceed, since SpO2 is acceptable on oxygen
questions.explanation: A rate of 6 with ETCO2 62 despite stimulation and repositioning is ventilatory failure, and supplemental oxygen is only hiding it. The next step is to support ventilation with positive pressure and lighten the sedative, escalating to an airway device or conversion if it does not correct. More oxygen leaves the CO2 untreated, and naloxone helps only if an opioid is involved.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: During cataract surgery under MAC, the patient becomes apneic and SpO2 falls to 86%. The face is draped and the surgeon is mid-procedure. What comes first?
options: Increase O2 under the drapes and observe
Ask the surgeon to finish the step first
Give flumazenil and naloxone together
Have the surgeon stop and expose the airway
questions.explanation: With apnea and falling saturation, the airway must be reached at once, so the surgeon stops, instruments come out of the eye, and the drapes come off to allow jaw thrust and bag-mask ventilation. More oxygen cannot help an apneic patient for long, and reversal agents take time and do not reverse propofol.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: Before MAC for a painful procedure, which discussion most directly prepares the patient for possible conversion of the anesthetic plan?
options: Deeper sedation or GA may be needed if MAC fails
Avoid mentioning conversion so as not to raise anxiety
Promise they will stay awake whatever happens
Conversion cannot happen once MAC has begun
questions.explanation: MAC requires a plan for rescue and possible conversion when the intended sedation level cannot safely meet procedural or patient needs. Discussing that possibility beforehand supports informed expectations and avoids presenting sedation depth as a guarantee.
questions.topic: Conversion to GA and patient expectations

questions.stem: After a 3-hour propofol infusion for TIVA, the patient still wakes within about 10 minutes of stopping it. Which property best explains this?
options: Active metabolites that oppose its hypnotic effect
Its context-sensitive half-time stays short
Renal excretion of unchanged drug within minutes
Rapid return of drug from fat to the blood
questions.explanation: Propofol is cleared rapidly, largely by the liver with extrahepatic contribution, so its context-sensitive half-time stays under about 40 minutes even after infusions lasting hours, and the small concentration drop needed for waking happens quickly. Its metabolites are inactive, renal excretion of unchanged drug is negligible, and drug returning from fat slows rather than speeds awakening.

questions.stem: Propofol produces hypnosis primarily through which receptor action?
options: Antagonism of NMDA glutamate receptors
Agonism at alpha-2 adrenergic receptors
Potentiation of GABA-A chloride currents
Agonism at presynaptic mu-opioid receptors
questions.explanation: Propofol enhances GABA-A receptor chloride conductance, hyperpolarizing neurons to produce hypnosis and amnesia. NMDA antagonism is ketamine's mechanism, alpha-2 agonism is dexmedetomidine's, and mu-opioid agonism belongs to the opioids, which explains why each of those drugs has a different side-effect profile.

questions.stem: An elderly hypovolemic patient with poor cardiac reserve becomes profoundly hypotensive after a propofol bolus tolerated by a younger healthy adult. Why?
options: Faster hepatic metabolism of propofol with age
Active metabolites that build up in older adults
Injection pain triggering a prolonged vagal response
Reduced reserve and volume magnify its vasodilation
questions.explanation: Propofol decreases systemic vascular tone and can depress myocardial performance, while older age, hypovolemia, limited cardiac reserve, and synergistic coadministered sedatives reduce tolerance of those effects. A bolus acceptable in a young euvolemic patient can therefore cause disproportionate hypotension in a frail hypovolemic patient. Propofol metabolites are inactive, and clearance falls rather than rises with age.

questions.stem: A patient with severe PONV after two prior anesthetics needs sedation for a 90-minute procedure. Which propofol property is most useful here?
options: Antiemetic effect at subhypnotic doses
Strong analgesia reducing opioid needs
Sympathetic stimulation preserving BP
Long-acting sedation into recovery
questions.explanation: Propofol has antiemetic activity, even at low subhypnotic infusion rates, which makes propofol-based sedation or TIVA a good choice for patients with a history of PONV. It is not an analgesic, so it does not reduce nausea by sparing opioids, and it lowers rather than raises blood pressure. Its quick offset is a strength, not prolonged sedation.

questions.stem: Which FOUR strategies can reduce propofol injection pain? (Select 4)
options: Pretreat with lidocaine using an effective technique
Use a hand vein to keep the antecubital free
Push the dose rapidly to shorten contact time
Inject more slowly
Use a larger proximal vein when possible
Administer through a well-running carrier IV
questions.explanation: Propofol injection pain falls when local concentration and endothelial contact are reduced or the vein is pretreated, so a larger proximal vein, a well-running carrier, slower injection, and lidocaine with venous occlusion all help. A rapid push into a small hand vein delivers the highest local concentration and hurts most.

questions.stem: Lidocaine 40 mg is pushed into a hand vein just before propofol, and the patient still reports burning. Which change makes the pretreatment more effective?
options: Give the lidocaine after the propofol instead
Double the lidocaine dose with no occlusion
Use a tourniquet hold for 30 to 60 seconds
Give lidocaine IV push 5 minutes earlier
questions.explanation: Lidocaine relieves propofol pain mainly by a local effect on the vein wall, and occluding venous outflow with a tourniquet for 30 to 60 seconds keeps it concentrated at the site, which works better than an unoccluded bolus. Giving it earlier lets it wash away, and giving it after propofol is too late for the first, most painful pass.

questions.stem: Which pharmacokinetic characteristic makes propofol easy to titrate for brief sedation?
options: A long fixed duration that smooths fluctuations
Active metabolites that sustain steady hypnosis
A specific reversal agent for instant waking
Fast onset and redistribution let effect change fast
questions.explanation: Propofol reaches the brain quickly and its clinical effect changes rapidly after bolus or infusion adjustments because of rapid distribution and redistribution. This permits relatively prompt titration of hypnotic depth during short procedures. Propofol has no active metabolites and no reversal agent.

questions.stem: Which THREE adverse effects should be anticipated after a large propofol bolus? (Select 3)
options: Respiratory depression
Hypotension
Apnea
Dissociative emergence reaction
Opioid chest-wall rigidity
Hypersalivation
questions.explanation: A large propofol bolus causes dose-dependent respiratory depression or apnea and hypotension from vasodilation and some myocardial depression. Emergence reactions and hypersalivation are characteristic of ketamine, and chest-wall rigidity of potent opioids, so they are not expected after propofol.

questions.stem: During intended moderate sedation, the patient becomes unresponsive to verbal commands and requires repeated airway maneuvers to maintain ventilation. What principle should guide management?
options: Rescue from the deeper level and reduce sedation
Continue, since the intended level was moderate
Wait for SpO2 to fall before airway support
Call it GA and add a paralytic to proceed
questions.explanation: Sedation depth can unintentionally progress beyond the intended level. The provider must recognize the actual clinical state and be capable of rescuing airway and ventilation while reducing or stopping sedative administration. The intended level does not govern management once the patient has gone deeper.

questions.stem: Why may backup IV access be valuable during prolonged deep propofol anesthesia/sedation when the only existing IV is difficult to observe?
options: Two IVs lower the risk of propofol hypotension
Losing the only IV stops hypnosis and rescue drugs
Propofol must run alone through a dedicated line
A second IV is what prevents propofol injection pain
questions.explanation: During TIVA or deep propofol sedation, an infiltrated or disconnected sole IV can cause sudden awareness and leaves no route for rescue drugs, and the problem may go unnoticed if the site is hidden. A second line or a visible, checked site guards against both. Extra IVs do not prevent hypotension, and injection pain depends on vein size and carrier flow.

questions.stem: An IV sedative has delayed onset and is followed by characteristic perineal paresthesia/pruritus. Which agent best fits?
options: Fospropofol
Propofol
Midazolam
Dexmedetomidine
questions.explanation: Fospropofol is a water-soluble prodrug that must be converted to propofol, so onset is delayed by several minutes. Perineal paresthesia and pruritus, likely from the phosphate released during conversion, are its characteristic side effects. Propofol acts quickly and causes injection pain instead, and dexmedetomidine and midazolam do not produce perineal symptoms.

questions.stem: Compared with direct propofol administration, why is fospropofol onset slower?
options: It is an NMDA antagonist with slow binding
It is stored in fat before it is released
It must first be converted to propofol
It needs renal activation to an active form
questions.explanation: Fospropofol has no hypnotic activity until alkaline phosphatases cleave it to propofol, so peak effect takes several minutes rather than the 1 to 2 minutes seen with propofol, and recovery is also slower. The conversion is enzymatic in plasma and tissues, not renal, and the drug is not an NMDA antagonist.

questions.stem: Fospropofol is converted to active propofol by which enzyme?
options: Plasma cholinesterase
Hepatic CYP2B6 oxidation
Tissue carboxylesterase
Alkaline phosphatase
questions.explanation: Fospropofol is a phosphate ester prodrug that endothelial alkaline phosphatases hydrolyze into propofol, phosphate, and formaldehyde, which is quickly converted to formate. That conversion step explains its slower onset. Carboxylesterases hydrolyze remimazolam, plasma cholinesterase hydrolyzes succinylcholine, and CYP2B6 helps metabolize propofol itself after it forms.

questions.stem: Fospropofol, a water-soluble propofol prodrug, received U.S. approval for MAC sedation in 2008. What is its practical status today?
options: The preferred agent for U.S. ICU sedation
No longer sold for U.S. clinical use
A first-line U.S. induction agent in adults
Approved now only for pediatric sedation
questions.explanation: Fospropofol was approved in the United States for MAC sedation but was later discontinued by the manufacturer, so it is not available for routine clinical use. It never became a standard ICU or induction agent, and it was not reapproved for a pediatric indication. Its delayed onset and perineal paresthesia limited its appeal.

questions.stem: After 3 days of ICU propofol at 80 mcg/kg/min, a patient develops metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, and a new right bundle branch block. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Sepsis-related lactic acidosis
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Propofol infusion syndrome
Hypertriglyceridemic pancreatitis
questions.explanation: Propofol infusion syndrome follows high-dose infusions, usually above 4 mg/kg/hr for more than 48 hours (80 mcg/kg/min is 4.8 mg/kg/hr), and presents with metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hyperkalemia, lipemia, arrhythmias such as new RBBB, and cardiac failure from impaired mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation. Hypertriglyceridemia and pancreatitis can occur with propofol but do not explain rhabdomyolysis and the ECG change.

questions.stem: Why does fospropofol produce less classic lipid-emulsion injection pain than propofol?
options: It blocks peripheral sodium channels locally
It contains lidocaine in the formulation
It is given intramuscularly, not IV
It is water soluble, unlike standard propofol
questions.explanation: Standard propofol is formulated in a lipid emulsion and commonly causes pain on injection. Fospropofol is water soluble and does not use the same lipid formulation, so classic propofol injection pain is reduced, although fospropofol has its own characteristic paresthesia and pruritus.

questions.stem: A fospropofol sedation protocol proposes pulse oximetry alone with no airway-rescue equipment. What is the major flaw?
options: It still forms propofol, which depresses breathing
A prodrug removes the risk of reaching deep sedation
Fospropofol has no effect on ventilation at all
Rescue gear is needed just for inhaled anesthetics
questions.explanation: Fospropofol becomes propofol in the body, so it carries the same dose-related respiratory depression, apnea, and hypotension, only with a slower onset that makes stacking doses more likely. Ventilation monitoring with capnography and immediate airway rescue are still required, and a slower onset is not a margin of safety.

questions.stem: For a brief outpatient procedure requiring rapid titration and rapid recovery, which agent generally best fits among these choices?
options: Dexmedetomidine
Fospropofol
Midazolam
Propofol
questions.explanation: Propofol's rapid onset and relatively rapid offset make it well suited to short procedures requiring frequent depth adjustments and prompt recovery. Dexmedetomidine and fospropofol have slower onset, while midazolam may produce less predictable or prolonged recovery in susceptible patients.

questions.stem: A patient receives midazolam before propofol and becomes apneic after a smaller propofol dose than expected. Which principle best explains this?
options: Midazolam displaces propofol from plasma proteins
Synergy lowers the propofol dose that causes apnea
Benzodiazepines speed propofol redistribution
Midazolam causes chest wall rigidity with propofol
questions.explanation: Midazolam and propofol both enhance inhibitory GABAergic effects, so coadministration reduces the propofol dose required for hypnosis while increasing respiratory depression beyond what either dose might cause alone. Dose requirements should therefore be reduced and titrated to effect when sedatives are combined. Chest wall rigidity is an opioid effect.

questions.stem: Propofol provides adequate hypnosis and amnesia, but the patient still responds strongly to incision. Which anesthetic component is missing?
options: Hypnosis
Amnesia
Analgesia
Muscle relaxation
questions.explanation: Propofol potentiates GABA-A receptors to produce hypnosis and amnesia but has essentially no analgesic effect, so a strong response to incision means nociception is not covered. Muscle relaxation is tempting because the patient moves, but blocking movement would hide the response without treating it; an opioid, ketamine, or local anesthetic supplies the missing analgesia.

questions.stem: After a propofol bolus, BP falls from 130/80 to 85/50, yet heart rate stays at 70/min. Why is there no reflex tachycardia?
options: Propofol directly stimulates the vagus nerve
Hypotension is too mild to trigger a reflex
Propofol acts as a beta-1 receptor antagonist
Propofol blunts the baroreceptor reflex
questions.explanation: Propofol lowers blood pressure through vasodilation and reduced sympathetic tone while also resetting and blunting the baroreceptor reflex, so the expected compensatory tachycardia does not appear. A 45 mmHg systolic drop would normally trigger a brisk reflex. Propofol has no beta-blocking action, and true vagal stimulation would slow the rate rather than hold it steady.

questions.stem: Only a small peripheral IV is available and propofol injection pain is anticipated. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Run a fast carrier, inject slowly, add lidocaine
Use the smallest distal vein to protect bigger ones
Inject quickly to shorten contact with the vein
Stop the carrier so the propofol is undiluted
questions.explanation: Propofol pain comes from free drug contacting the vein wall, so a fast-running carrier and slow injection dilute it, and lidocaine pretreatment with venous occlusion blocks the local response. A rapid push or stopping the carrier raises the local concentration, and a small distal vein makes the pain worse.

questions.stem: An 80-kg patient receives propofol at 100 mcg/kg/min from a 10 mg/mL solution. What pump rate is required?
options: 48 mL/hr
8 mL/hr
80 mL/hr
480 mL/hr
questions.explanation: 100 mcg/kg/min × 80 kg = 8,000 mcg/min, or 8 mg/min. Over an hour that is 8 × 60 = 480 mg/hr, and at 10 mg/mL the pump rate is 480 ÷ 10 = 48 mL/hr. Choosing 480 mL/hr forgets to divide by concentration, and 8 mL/hr uses mg/min as mL/hr.

questions.stem: Why is loss of purposeful responsiveness during propofol sedation clinically important?
options: It shows that analgesia has become adequate
It may mark the shift to general anesthesia depth
It signals tachyphylaxis to the propofol infusion
It means protective airway reflexes are intact
questions.explanation: Loss of purposeful response even to painful stimulation meets the responsiveness criterion for general anesthesia rather than deep sedation. With propofol, this transition can occur quickly and brings an increasing likelihood of airway obstruction and inadequate spontaneous ventilation, with protective reflexes becoming less reliable.

questions.stem: Before propofol sedation, a patient reports hives after eating eggs as a child. How does this history affect propofol use?
options: Propofol is contraindicated; use etomidate
Premedicate with steroids before propofol
Propofol can generally be used safely
Use fospropofol, which lacks egg lecithin
questions.explanation: Propofol emulsion contains egg lecithin, a purified yolk phosphatide, but most egg allergies are to proteins such as ovalbumin, and patients with egg allergy rarely react to propofol, so it can generally be used. Routine steroid premedication is not recommended for this history. Fospropofol is no longer marketed, so it is not a practical substitute.

questions.stem: A propofol infusion is running at 50 mcg/kg/min. The procedure becomes more stimulating and the patient begins purposeful movement without airway obstruction. Which response best reflects rational titration?
options: Hold the rate, since the calculated dose is fixed
Double the rate at once without reassessment
Add a paralytic and keep the same rate
Increase the rate in steps while reassessing
questions.explanation: Propofol should be titrated to clinical effect because stimulation, age, comorbidity, and coadministered drugs change dose requirements. Incremental adjustment with repeated assessment of responsiveness, ventilation, and blood pressure is safer than treating a calculated infusion rate as a fixed endpoint. A paralytic would hide movement without treating its cause.

questions.stem: A patient with severe OSA requires cooperative sedation while preservation of spontaneous ventilation is especially important. Which agent may be advantageous because it causes relatively little respiratory depression?
options: Dexmedetomidine
Propofol
Midazolam
Remifentanil
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine generally causes less respiratory depression than propofol, benzodiazepines, or opioids and can be useful when cooperative sedation and spontaneous ventilation are priorities. OSA still requires careful airway monitoring because no sedative eliminates obstruction risk.

questions.stem: For sedation in severe OSA, which dexmedetomidine tradeoff should be anticipated?
options: Less respiratory depression, slower onset, bradycardia
Rapid onset with frequent apnea at usual doses
Strong opioid-like analgesia with chest wall rigidity
Hypertension and tachycardia from sympathetic surge
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine tends to preserve ventilation better than many sedatives, but onset can be slow and clinically important bradycardia and hypotension may occur, especially with loading doses or in susceptible patients. Its analgesic effect is modest, and it lowers rather than raises sympathetic tone once the brief loading-dose hypertension passes.

questions.stem: After a dexmedetomidine loading dose, marked bradycardia and hypotension develop without respiratory depression. Which explanation best fits?
options: Opioid-like chest wall rigidity after the load
Expected alpha-2 agonist hemodynamic effects
Anaphylaxis to the dexmedetomidine vehicle
Propofol-like direct myocardial depression
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine lowers central sympathetic outflow through alpha-2A receptors, so bradycardia and hypotension are expected, especially after a rapid load or in volume-depleted patients, while ventilation is largely spared. Anaphylaxis would bring bronchospasm, rash, and tachycardia rather than bradycardia, and dexmedetomidine does not cause chest wall rigidity.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient is ordered dexmedetomidine 1 mcg/kg over 10 minutes from a 4 mcg/mL solution. What pump rate delivers the loading dose?
options: 10.5 mL/hr for 10 minutes
17.5 mL/hr for 10 minutes
70 mL/hr for 10 minutes
105 mL/hr for 10 minutes
questions.explanation: The load is 1 mcg/kg × 70 kg = 70 mcg, and at 4 mcg/mL that is 70 ÷ 4 = 17.5 mL. Giving 17.5 mL over 10 minutes means 17.5 × 6 = 105 mL/hr for 10 minutes. Choosing 17.5 mL/hr treats the volume as an hourly rate, which would take an hour to give the load.

questions.stem: A patient with renal dysfunction needs brief benzodiazepine sedation with rapid recovery. Which agent is rapidly hydrolyzed by carboxylesterase metabolism and has an inactive metabolite?
options: Remimazolam
Midazolam
Lorazepam
Diazepam
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is an ultra-short-acting benzodiazepine hydrolyzed primarily by carboxylesterase 1 to a metabolite with very low pharmacologic activity. Renal impairment has relatively little effect on parent-drug disposition, although severe hepatic impairment can reduce clearance and prolong recovery.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes remimazolam disposition?
options: Renal excretion of the unchanged parent drug
CYP3A4 oxidation to an active hydroxy metabolite
Rapid carboxylesterase hydrolysis, inactive product
Hofmann elimination independent of organ function
questions.explanation: Remimazolam undergoes rapid carboxylesterase-mediated hydrolysis, producing an inactive metabolite. Renal impairment has limited effect on the parent drug, whereas severe hepatic impairment can slow clearance and prolong recovery. CYP3A4 oxidation to an active metabolite describes midazolam, and Hofmann elimination describes cisatracurium.

questions.stem: After remimazolam plus fentanyl, a patient is somnolent and hypoventilating. Which antagonist reverses the benzodiazepine component specifically?
options: Sugammadex
Naloxone
Flumazenil
Physostigmine
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is a benzodiazepine, so flumazenil competitively displaces it at the GABA-A benzodiazepine site, while naloxone is needed for the fentanyl component. Sugammadex binds steroidal neuromuscular blockers and physostigmine treats central anticholinergic syndrome, so neither reverses sedation from these drugs.

questions.stem: For colonoscopy sedation in a frail ASA III patient, which advantage of remimazolam over propofol is best supported?
options: Stronger analgesia during the procedure
No respiratory depression even with fentanyl
Faster onset to peak effect than propofol
Less hypotension at equivalent sedation
questions.explanation: Trials comparing remimazolam with propofol for procedural sedation show less hypotension and less need for vasopressors, which suits patients with limited reserve. It still depresses ventilation, especially with an opioid, provides no analgesia, and its onset is similar to or slightly slower than that of propofol.

questions.stem: A frail patient with limited hemodynamic reserve requires brief benzodiazepine sedation and predictable recovery. Which option may offer less prolonged accumulation than conventional longer-acting benzodiazepines?
options: Remimazolam
Lorazepam
Diazepam
Midazolam
questions.explanation: Remimazolam's rapid carboxylesterase-mediated hydrolysis limits accumulation and supports predictable recovery compared with conventional benzodiazepines. Midazolam is the tempting choice, but repeated doses accumulate with its active metabolite, and lorazepam and diazepam last far longer. Remimazolam can still cause hypotension and respiratory depression, so frailty still warrants careful titration.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements about remimazolam are correct? (Select 2)
options: It acts at GABA-A receptors as a benzodiazepine
Its benzodiazepine effects can be antagonized by flumazenil
It provides strong intrinsic analgesia
It cannot depress ventilation
It depends primarily on renal excretion for termination
It has a long context-sensitive offset
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is an ester-metabolized benzodiazepine that acts at GABA-A receptors, so flumazenil can antagonize it. It provides no analgesia, has a short offset because tissue esterases clear it rather than the kidneys, and can still depress ventilation, especially with opioids.

questions.stem: Resedation after flumazenil is a greater concern after reversing midazolam than after reversing remimazolam. Why?
options: Flumazenil binds remimazolam more tightly
Flumazenil can wear off before midazolam does
Remimazolam is reversed by esterases, not flumazenil
Flumazenil is metabolized faster with midazolam present
questions.explanation: Flumazenil has a short duration, roughly 30 to 60 minutes, so after reversing a longer-acting drug such as midazolam the agonist can outlast it and sedation returns. Remimazolam is hydrolyzed quickly, so its effect often fades before flumazenil wears off. Both drugs are reversed by flumazenil at the same benzodiazepine binding site.

questions.stem: After midazolam 2 mg and fentanyl 100 mcg, the patient is arousable but RR is 4/min; airway support has started. Which antagonist most directly restores respiratory drive?
options: Flumazenil
Physostigmine
Naloxone
Sugammadex
questions.explanation: Opioids depress the brainstem response to CO2 and cause the slow respiratory rate, so naloxone most directly restores drive, while flumazenil reverses the benzodiazepine sedation that adds to it synergistically. Both may be needed, but naloxone addresses the low rate. Sugammadex and physostigmine do not reverse either drug.

questions.stem: A patient in septic shock for 5 days receives ketamine for a bedside procedure, and blood pressure falls further. What is the best explanation?
options: Ketamine blocks alpha-1 receptors at high doses
Ketamine releases histamine, causing vasodilation
Emergence agitation raises myocardial oxygen demand
Depleted catecholamines unmask myocardial depression
questions.explanation: Ketamine normally raises blood pressure indirectly by stimulating sympathetic outflow and blocking catecholamine reuptake, but it is a direct myocardial depressant. In prolonged critical illness with depleted catecholamine stores, the indirect support is lost and the direct depression shows, so blood pressure can fall. Ketamine is not an alpha blocker and causes little histamine release.

questions.stem: Which THREE effects are commonly associated with ketamine? (Select 3)
options: Increased secretions
Marked dose-independent hypotension
Increased heart rate/blood pressure in many patients
Emergence phenomena
Opioid chest-wall rigidity
Bronchoconstriction
questions.explanation: Ketamine commonly causes sympathetic stimulation with higher heart rate and blood pressure, increased salivation, and emergence phenomena. It bronchodilates rather than constricting the airways, hypotension occurs mainly in catecholamine-depleted patients, and chest-wall rigidity is an opioid effect.

questions.stem: Ketamine sedation is planned for four otherwise healthy children. Which procedure carries the highest risk of laryngospasm?
options: Removing a foreign body from the oropharynx
Closed reduction of a forearm fracture
Laceration repair on the scalp
Lumbar puncture in the lateral position
questions.explanation: Laryngospasm with ketamine is more likely when the oropharynx or larynx is stimulated by instruments, blood, or secretions, so procedures inside the mouth or pharynx carry the highest risk, as does an active respiratory infection. Extremity and scalp procedures do not stimulate the airway, which is why ketamine is widely used for fracture reductions and laceration repairs.

questions.stem: Why can ketamine plus propofol be useful for a brief painful procedure?
options: Propofol supplies the analgesia that ketamine lacks
Ketamine adds analgesia; propofol adds titratable hypnosis
Both agents reliably raise blood pressure together
The combination removes respiratory risk entirely
questions.explanation: The drugs complement rather than duplicate each other: ketamine supplies analgesia and sympathetic support, while propofol supplies rapidly titratable hypnosis and can blunt some ketamine emergence effects. The combination still requires careful titration because respiratory and hemodynamic complications remain possible.

questions.stem: A brief intensely painful stimulus requires an opioid that can be titrated rapidly and wears off quickly when stopped. Which choice best fits, with respiratory depression as the major tradeoff?
options: Hydromorphone
Morphine
Remifentanil
Methadone
questions.explanation: Remifentanil is rapidly metabolized by nonspecific blood and tissue esterases, giving it a very short context-sensitive half-time and allowing rapid adjustment to brief painful stimulation. That same potency can cause abrupt respiratory depression or apnea, so ventilation must be closely monitored.

questions.stem: After a rapid large fentanyl bolus, bag-mask ventilation becomes very difficult even with jaw thrust and an oral airway, and the thorax and abdomen feel board-like. What complication should be suspected?
options: Bronchospasm from histamine release
Laryngospasm at the vocal cords
Negative-pressure pulmonary edema
Opioid-induced chest-wall rigidity
questions.explanation: Rapid administration of a large fentanyl dose can cause marked truncal and chest-wall rigidity that makes ventilation difficult even when the upper airway is open. Fentanyl releases little histamine, and laryngospasm would be an upper-airway problem. Management restores ventilation, with naloxone or neuromuscular blockade according to severity and setting.

questions.stem: During remifentanil sedation, RR falls to 6/min and ETCO2 rises. What is the immediate priority?
options: Reduce the infusion and support ventilation
Increase the infusion to ease the distress
Give flumazenil to restore respiratory drive
Wait, since the effect wears off in minutes
questions.explanation: Remifentanil depresses ventilation in a dose-dependent way, so the response to a rate of 6 with rising ETCO2 is to lower or stop the infusion while supporting the airway and breathing. Its short context-sensitive half-time means the effect fades within minutes after stopping, but that does not make waiting safe while the patient hypoventilates. Flumazenil does not reverse opioids.

questions.stem: After a 6-hour fentanyl infusion, the patient takes much longer to recover than after a single bolus. What best explains this?
options: It forms an active metabolite, norfentanyl
Its context-sensitive half-time grows
Plasma esterases saturate during infusion
Renal clearance falls as the infusion runs
questions.explanation: Fentanyl is highly lipid soluble, so during long infusions it fills peripheral tissues, and after stopping, drug returns to plasma and slows the fall in concentration; its context-sensitive half-time climbs steeply after a few hours. Norfentanyl is inactive, and esterase metabolism describes remifentanil, whose half-time stays about 3 to 4 minutes regardless of duration.

questions.stem: Which FOUR agents provide clinically meaningful analgesia as part of a sedation technique? (Select 4)
options: Fentanyl
Remifentanil
Ketamine
Sufentanil
Propofol
Midazolam
questions.explanation: Fentanyl, remifentanil, and sufentanil are opioid analgesics, and ketamine provides substantial analgesia through NMDA receptor antagonism. Propofol and midazolam provide hypnosis, sedation, or amnesia but no reliable procedural analgesia, so painful steps under propofol alone can cause movement.

questions.stem: A patient has a severe history of distressing hallucinations during prior dissociative sedation. Which agent is least attractive if alternatives meet the procedural goals?
options: Dexmedetomidine
Propofol
Ketamine
Remifentanil
questions.explanation: Ketamine's NMDA antagonism produces dissociation, and emergence reactions such as vivid dreams, hallucinations, and agitation are its characteristic adverse effect, more common in adults and with larger doses. A patient with a severe prior reaction is better served by an alternative such as dexmedetomidine, propofol, or an opioid technique. Benzodiazepine premedication can reduce but not reliably prevent recurrence.

questions.stem: During cooperative sedation for carotid angiography, HR falls to 42/min shortly after starting the sedative. Which agent most strongly fits this adverse-effect profile?
options: Midazolam
Ketamine
Remimazolam
Dexmedetomidine
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine stimulates central alpha-2A receptors and reduces sympathetic outflow, so a heart rate falling to the low 40s shortly after starting the sedative fits it best, often with hypotension after a loading dose. Ketamine tends to raise heart rate and blood pressure, and midazolam and remimazolam more often cause mild hypotension with little change in heart rate.

questions.stem: Midazolam 1 mg IV is given for procedural sedation. About how long should you wait before judging its effect and redosing?
options: About 30 seconds
About 15 to 20 minutes
About 3 to 5 minutes
About 60 seconds
questions.explanation: Midazolam reaches peak effect about 3 to 5 minutes after an IV dose, so redosing sooner stacks doses before the first has peaked and risks oversedation. A 30- to 60-second interval fits propofol, not midazolam, and waiting 15 to 20 minutes slows titration without adding safety.

questions.stem: A patient taking ritonavir-boosted HIV therapy stays deeply sedated for hours after a modest IV midazolam dose. What best explains this?
options: CYP3A4 induction creating more active metabolite
Ritonavir displacing midazolam from albumin
Additive GABA-A agonism by ritonavir itself
CYP3A4 inhibition slowing midazolam clearance
questions.explanation: Ritonavir is a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor, and midazolam depends on CYP3A4 for clearance, so its levels and duration rise sharply; the combination is contraindicated with oral midazolam and calls for caution and reduced IV doses. Induction would shorten the effect, and protein-binding displacement causes at most a brief rise in free drug.

questions.stem: Flumazenil is being considered for oversedation after a procedure. Which history most raises the risk of seizures if it is given?
options: Fentanyl given for procedural pain
Daily alprazolam for panic disorder
One oral midazolam dose before surgery
Controlled hypertension on a beta-blocker
questions.explanation: Flumazenil can precipitate acute withdrawal and seizures in patients physically dependent on benzodiazepines, so daily alprazolam use is the main warning sign. A single oral midazolam dose does not create dependence, and fentanyl is not affected by flumazenil. In a dependent patient, support ventilation instead or titrate very small flumazenil doses.

questions.stem: A dexmedetomidine loading infusion begins only a few minutes before the procedure, and the patient remains alert. Which property best explains the delayed effect?
options: It needs hepatic conversion to an active form
It sedates only when given with an opioid
Its onset is slower than that of propofol
It causes paradoxical arousal at first
questions.explanation: A dexmedetomidine load is usually given over about 10 minutes, and sedation builds over that period, so starting it minutes before stimulation leaves the patient alert. That slower onset is the tradeoff for limited respiratory depression. It is active as given, needs no opioid to sedate, and does not cause obligatory paradoxical arousal.

questions.stem: Dexmedetomidine is chosen for sedation during awake fiberoptic intubation. Which of its properties is most helpful here?
options: Rapid onset within 30 seconds of a small bolus
Analgesia strong enough to replace topicalization
Reliable amnesia for the entire airway procedure
Sedation with preserved breathing and less saliva
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine keeps the patient cooperative and breathing spontaneously, and its antisialagogue effect dries secretions, which helps the fiberoptic view. Topical anesthesia of the airway is still needed because its analgesia is modest, and amnesia is less reliable than with benzodiazepines. Its onset takes minutes, so the load is started early.

questions.stem: After ketamine, copious oral secretions complicate airway management. Which drug effect is responsible?
options: Increased salivation
Laryngeal reflex loss
Gastric regurgitation
Anticholinergic effect
questions.explanation: Ketamine increases salivary and tracheobronchial secretions, which can trigger coughing or laryngospasm, so an antisialagogue such as glycopyrrolate is sometimes given. An anticholinergic effect would dry secretions, the opposite finding, and ketamine largely preserves laryngeal reflexes rather than abolishing them.

questions.stem: Which sedative-analgesic produces dissociation primarily through NMDA-receptor antagonism?
options: Remimazolam
Dexmedetomidine
Ketamine
Propofol
questions.explanation: Ketamine primarily antagonizes NMDA glutamate receptors, producing a dissociative state with both sedation and analgesia. This distinguishes it from GABAergic hypnotics such as propofol and benzodiazepines, which do not provide comparable intrinsic analgesia.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient receives remifentanil 0.1 mcg/kg/min from a 50 mcg/mL solution. What pump rate is required?
options: 1.4 mL/hr
0.14 mL/hr
84 mL/hr
8.4 mL/hr
questions.explanation: 0.1 mcg/kg/min x 70 kg = 7 mcg/min, and 7 x 60 = 420 mcg/hr. Dividing by 50 mcg/mL gives 8.4 mL/hr. Forgetting to convert minutes to hours gives 0.14 mL/hr, and a decimal slip gives 84 or 1.4 mL/hr.

questions.stem: Dexmedetomidine produces arousable sedation that resembles natural non-REM sleep. Where does it act to produce this?
options: GABA-A receptors in the cerebral cortex
Alpha-2 receptors in the locus coeruleus
NMDA receptors in thalamocortical tracts
Mu-opioid receptors in the brainstem
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine acts on alpha-2A receptors in the locus coeruleus, reducing noradrenergic output and producing a state close to non-REM sleep from which patients can be roused to cooperate. GABA-A modulation is how propofol and benzodiazepines work, NMDA antagonism is ketamine, and mu-opioid agonism belongs to the opioids.

questions.stem: Which THREE effects are expected from midazolam during procedural sedation? (Select 3)
options: Anxiolysis
Sedation
Anterograde amnesia
Analgesia
Dissociation
Neuromuscular blockade
questions.explanation: Midazolam acts on GABA-A receptors to provide anxiolysis, sedation, and anterograde amnesia. It does not provide meaningful analgesia or dissociation and has no neuromuscular blocking effect, though at high doses it can relax muscles centrally and depress breathing, especially with opioids.

questions.stem: How does fentanyl change the ventilatory response to carbon dioxide?
options: Shifts the curve left, raising ventilation at any CO2
Leaves the curve unchanged but lowers tidal volume
Shifts the CO2 response curve right and flattens it
Steepens the curve but raises the apneic threshold
questions.explanation: Opioids depress brainstem chemoreceptor sensitivity, so the CO2 response curve shifts to the right and its slope flattens; a higher PaCO2 is needed for the same ventilation, and the apneic threshold rises. Benzodiazepines mainly flatten the slope, which is why the combination depresses ventilation more than either alone. A left shift is what hypoxemia or metabolic acidosis produces.

questions.stem: Propofol and remifentanil are combined for deep sedation. Which paired adverse effects deserve particular anticipation?
options: Emergence hallucinations and hypersalivation
Bradycardia with preserved breathing
Hypertension and tachycardia
Hypotension and respiratory depression/apnea
questions.explanation: Propofol causes dose-dependent hypotension and respiratory depression, and remifentanil adds synergistic respiratory depression, apnea, and some further hypotension. Hallucinations, hypersalivation, hypertension, and tachycardia describe ketamine, and bradycardia with preserved breathing describes dexmedetomidine, so those pairings belong to other agents.

questions.stem: Facial surgery with electrocautery is planned under MAC after an alcohol-based skin prep. Which step most reduces the fire risk from the prep?
options: Apply it generously so it covers well
Let the prep dry fully before draping
Drape at once to keep the prep sterile
Raise oxygen flow to dilute the vapors
questions.explanation: Alcohol-based preps are flammable, and vapor trapped under drapes adds fuel beside the oxygen and the cautery tip, so the prep must dry completely and pooled solution must be removed before draping. Draping immediately traps the vapor, and raising oxygen flow enriches the atmosphere rather than diluting the hazard.

questions.stem: During facial MAC with open oxygen, which setup most increases fire risk?
options: Nasal cannula flow set at 2 L/min
Drapes kept flat and open to room air
Tented drapes pooling oxygen by cautery
Oxygen delivered through a sealed LMA
questions.explanation: Tented facial drapes trap supplemental oxygen, creating an oxygen-enriched pocket right beside the electrocautery. Low nasal flow with open, flat drapes lets oxygen disperse, and a sealed LMA keeps oxygen inside the breathing system, so both lower the oxidizer component of fire risk.

questions.stem: During facial MAC with nasal oxygen, the drapes near the cautery tip catch fire. What should be done first?
options: Call for a CO2 extinguisher before acting
Increase oxygen to support the patient
Finish the cautery step, then assess the field
Stop oxygen flow and remove burning drapes
questions.explanation: For a fire on or near the patient, ASA guidance is to stop the flow of airway gases and remove burning drapes and materials at once, then extinguish them with saline or water and assess the patient. Turning oxygen up feeds the fire, and waiting for an extinguisher delays steps that work in seconds.

questions.stem: A patient having facial surgery with electrocautery needs FiO2 above 30% to keep SpO2 above 92%. What does ASA fire guidance recommend?
options: Secure the airway with an LMA or tube
Raise nasal flow and tent the drapes higher
Deliver 100% oxygen by face mask under drapes
Switch nasal oxygen to a simple face mask
questions.explanation: ASA fire prevention guidance says that if a patient near an ignition source needs oxygen above about 30% to stay saturated, the airway should be secured with a tracheal tube or supraglottic device so oxygen goes into a closed system rather than the field. Higher open flows, masks, or tented drapes all raise oxygen concentration around the ignition source.

questions.stem: During MAC, regurgitation occurs and the patient acutely desaturates. What is the immediate priority?
options: Raise nasal oxygen and finish the procedure
Stop, suction, position, and support ventilation
Give flumazenil before assessing the airway
Wait for coughing to clear the airway on its own
questions.explanation: Suspected aspiration requires immediate airway-focused management: stop the procedure as feasible, suction and position the patient, restore oxygenation and ventilation, and secure the airway when clinically necessary. More oxygen or reversal agents do not clear material from the airway.

questions.stem: Which THREE findings most strongly support clinically significant aspiration during MAC? (Select 3)
options: ETCO2 rising from 38 to 44 mmHg
New cough, wheeze, or abnormal breath sounds
Brief bradycardia during scope insertion
New hypoxemia
Witnessed regurgitation/vomiting
Brief cough during scope insertion
questions.explanation: Witnessed regurgitation or vomiting, new hypoxemia, and new cough, wheeze, or abnormal breath sounds support clinically significant aspiration. A brief cough with scope passage, a modest ETCO2 rise with sedation, and vagal bradycardia during insertion are expected during endoscopy and do not point to aspiration.

questions.stem: During a lidocaine field block under light sedation, the patient reports a metallic taste and ringing in the ears, then becomes agitated. What is the best next step?
options: Finish the block, then reassess the symptoms
Give a large propofol bolus for agitation
Stop injecting and prepare to treat LAST
Treat it as anxiety and reassure the patient
questions.explanation: Metallic taste, tinnitus, and new agitation during injection are early CNS signs of local anesthetic systemic toxicity, so injection stops at once, help and the lipid emulsion kit are called for, and airway and seizure management are prepared. Finishing the block adds more drug, and large propofol doses can worsen cardiovascular depression; benzodiazepines are preferred for seizures.

questions.stem: A deeply sedated patient becomes hypotensive after repeated propofol boluses. Which mechanism is most likely?
options: Vagal reflex from procedural stimulation of viscera
Upper-airway obstruction with rising hypercapnia
Anaphylaxis to the soybean and egg emulsion
Dose-related vasodilation and myocardial depression
questions.explanation: Propofol reduces systemic vascular resistance and can depress myocardial contractility, so repeated boluses cause dose-related hypotension. The effect is amplified by hypovolemia, advanced age, limited cardiac reserve, and other sedative or vasodilating drugs. Anaphylaxis would bring bronchospasm, rash, and tachycardia, and hypercapnia tends to raise blood pressure.

questions.stem: A patient becomes apneic immediately after an opioid bolus during MAC. What should be addressed first?
options: Airway and ventilation first, then reduce the opioid
Flumazenil first, then check the airway and breathing
More oxygen flow without checking ventilation
Observation, since opioid apnea is brief
questions.explanation: Opioid-induced apnea is first managed by restoring airway patency and effective ventilation. Opioid administration should be reduced or stopped and naloxone considered when clinically indicated. Flumazenil does not reverse opioids, and oxygen does nothing for an apneic patient until ventilation resumes.

questions.stem: During sedation, jaw thrust relieves snoring, but obstruction returns whenever it is released. The patient still gags to oral suction. Which adjunct is best?
options: Oropharyngeal airway
Nasopharyngeal airway
Supraglottic airway
Endotracheal tube
questions.explanation: A nasopharyngeal airway is tolerated by patients with intact gag reflexes and holds the tongue and soft palate off the posterior pharynx, keeping the airway open without constant jaw thrust. An oral airway in a patient who still gags can trigger vomiting or laryngospasm, and a supraglottic device or tube is more than this level of sedation needs.

questions.stem: Jaw thrust and airway repositioning fail; obstruction persists and oxygenation is worsening. What is the next priority?
options: Higher-flow nasal oxygen and continued observation
Naloxone and wait for spontaneous breathing
Bag-mask ventilation, escalating to a device
Repeat jaw thrust until SpO2 recovers alone
questions.explanation: When jaw thrust and repositioning fail and oxygenation worsens, the patient needs active positive-pressure ventilation with bag-mask, adding an oral or nasal airway, supraglottic device, or tube as needed. More oxygen cannot pass a closed airway, and reversal agents take time and do not fix mechanical obstruction or propofol effect.

questions.stem: A sedated patient begins actively vomiting during MAC. Which position best limits aspiration while the pharynx is suctioned?
options: Supine and flat with the neck extended
Head-up sitting with the neck flexed
Prone with the head turned to one side
Lateral and head-down for drainage
questions.explanation: During active vomiting, turning the patient to the side and lowering the head lets material drain out of the mouth instead of into the trachea while suction clears the pharynx. Head-up positioning helps prevent passive regurgitation before it happens, but once vomitus is in the pharynx it directs it toward the larynx. Flat supine is the worst position for drainage.

questions.stem: During MAC in a remote location, severe hypotension develops and no vasopressor or emergency drug is immediately available. Which systems failure is exposed?
options: Remote site lacked OR-level rescue preparedness
Vasopressors are rarely needed during MAC
Remote sites need fewer rescue drugs than ORs
Monitoring alone should catch hypotension early
questions.explanation: Remote anesthetizing locations must support the same essential rescue functions as the operating room, including appropriate monitoring, oxygenation and ventilation equipment, emergency drugs, and airway capability. Severe hypotension without an immediately available vasopressor shows a system-level preparedness failure, and monitoring can detect hypotension but cannot treat it.

questions.stem: A patient becomes profoundly bradycardic and hypotensive after dexmedetomidine. What should occur first?
options: Continue if SpO2 is normal and recheck later
Stop the infusion, assess perfusion, and treat
Give more dexmedetomidine to deepen sedation
Give flumazenil to reverse the alpha-2 effect
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine can cause clinically important bradycardia and hypotension. Reduce or stop the infusion, assess perfusion, and treat with anticholinergics, fluids, or vasopressors based on severity. Flumazenil acts only at benzodiazepine sites, and a normal SpO2 says nothing about perfusion.

questions.stem: During ketamine sedation, laryngospasm develops despite previously preserved spontaneous ventilation. What does this illustrate?
options: Laryngospasm is a propofol effect, not ketamine
Capnography sampling lines trigger laryngospasm
Breathing on its own does not mean reflexes are safe
Laryngospasm means the ketamine dose was too low
questions.explanation: Ketamine often preserves spontaneous respiratory drive, but preserved breathing is not the same as a guaranteed airway or intact protective reflexes. Secretions, vomiting, obstruction, apnea, and laryngospasm can still occur, so full airway monitoring and rescue capability remain necessary.

questions.stem: After a sedative bolus, the patient becomes unresponsive, apneic, and hypotensive. Which transition should be assumed until proven otherwise?
options: Stable moderate sedation after the bolus
Drift back toward minimal sedation
Isolated analgesia without hypnosis
Progression to general anesthesia depth
questions.explanation: Unresponsiveness to stimulation with apnea indicates general anesthesia depth on the sedation continuum, and hypotension further signals significant anesthetic effect that requires immediate physiologic support. Moderate sedation requires a purposeful response to voice or light touch with adequate spontaneous ventilation.

questions.stem: During prone MAC, repeated obstruction occurs and access to the head is poor. What should be reconsidered before simply giving more sedative?
options: Whether a secured airway is now safer
Whether capnography should be removed
Whether more sedative will improve pharyngeal tone
Whether access matters only after desaturation
questions.explanation: Prone positioning restricts immediate access to the face and can delay basic or advanced airway rescue. Recurrent obstruction in that setting means the margin for further deepening is small and should prompt consideration of a secured airway before deterioration. More sedative lowers pharyngeal tone rather than improving it.

questions.stem: In a high-fire-risk facial procedure, why does inspired oxygen concentration near the field matter?
options: Fire risk tracks total gas flow, not oxygen
It lowers ignition energy and speeds burning
Oxygen itself acts as the fuel in the fire
Higher oxygen keeps drapes from igniting
questions.explanation: Higher local oxygen concentration makes materials ignite more easily and burn more intensely even though oxygen itself is not the fuel. When an ignition source such as electrocautery is close to drapes or other fuel, oxygen enrichment near the field materially increases fire risk.

questions.stem: A remote-procedure team has no predetermined way to stop the procedure and gain airway access during an emergency. Which safety element is missing?
options: A plan for postoperative nausea and vomiting
A plan for routine neuromuscular blockade
A plan for stopping work and reaching the airway
A lower SpO2 alarm limit on the oximeter
questions.explanation: Remote or access-limited procedures need an executable rescue plan agreed on before starting: who stops the procedure, how equipment is moved away, and how the anesthesia team reaches and manages the airway. Nausea prophylaxis and alarm settings matter, but neither gets anyone to the airway in an emergency.

questions.stem: A MAC safety plan focuses only on apnea and obstruction. Which additional hazards still require explicit preparation?
options: Postoperative nausea and recall as main concerns
Awareness and patient dissatisfaction afterward
Nothing more once capnography is in use
Aspiration, laryngospasm, instability, LAST, and fire
questions.explanation: A complete MAC rescue plan must extend beyond hypoventilation and obstruction. Aspiration, laryngospasm, hemodynamic collapse, local anesthetic systemic toxicity when local anesthetics are used, and surgical fire in oxygen-enriched fields can all require immediate, rehearsed intervention.

questions.stem: During MAC, snoring and paradoxical chest movement develop while a capnogram is still present. What is the best first intervention?
options: Head repositioning and jaw thrust
IV lidocaine to blunt airway reflexes
Deeper sedation to relax the patient
Watch until the SpO2 begins to fall
questions.explanation: Snoring and paradoxical chest movement indicate inspiratory effort against a partially obstructed upper airway. Head repositioning and jaw thrust directly relieve pharyngeal collapse and are preferable to increasing sedative depth, which further reduces airway tone. Waiting for desaturation wastes the warning the capnogram provides.

questions.stem: During MAC, mask ventilation remains inadequate despite an oral airway and a two-hand technique, and SpO2 is 82%. What is the next step?
options: Increase nasal cannula oxygen flow
Place a supraglottic airway
Give flumazenil and naloxone
Wait for spontaneous breathing to return
questions.explanation: When face-mask ventilation fails despite an oral airway and a two-hand technique, the difficult airway algorithm moves to a supraglottic airway, which bypasses pharyngeal obstruction and usually restores ventilation quickly. Nasal oxygen cannot overcome obstruction, reversal agents take minutes and do not reverse propofol, and waiting at an SpO2 of 82% risks hypoxic injury.

questions.stem: During MAC for TAVR in severe aortic stenosis, propofol drops BP to 80/45 mmHg with HR 70/min. Which treatment best fits the physiology?
options: Ephedrine to raise heart rate and BP
Nitroglycerin to reduce LV wall stress
Phenylephrine to restore afterload
Fluid bolus alone, avoiding vasopressors
questions.explanation: In severe aortic stenosis, coronary perfusion depends on diastolic pressure and the hypertrophied ventricle tolerates tachycardia poorly, so propofol-induced vasodilation is treated with a pure alpha agonist such as phenylephrine that restores afterload without raising heart rate. Ephedrine adds tachycardia, nitroglycerin lowers pressure further, and fluid alone is too slow and limited.

questions.stem: During facial MAC with nasal oxygen at 4 L/min, the surgeon is about to use electrocautery near the face. What should be done first?
options: Stop or lower O2 about a minute before
Raise O2 flow to keep SpO2 high during it
Switch to a face mask under the drapes
Stop O2 at the moment cautery starts
questions.explanation: ASA fire guidance is to stop or reduce supplemental oxygen for about a minute before an ignition source is used near the face, so the oxygen-enriched pocket under the drapes can disperse. Stopping flow at the moment of activation leaves the enriched gas in place, and a face mask under drapes concentrates oxygen further.

questions.stem: A patient receives IV lidocaine plus a large local field block. What should be tracked most carefully?
options: The IV lidocaine dose, since infiltration is local
Cumulative local anesthetic dose and LAST signs
The surgeon's infiltrated dose, since IV is small
The propofol concentration at the effect site
questions.explanation: Systemic toxicity depends on total local anesthetic exposure, absorption rate, injection site, and patient factors, not on whether the drug was given intravenously or infiltrated. Combining IV lidocaine with a large field block therefore requires tracking the cumulative dose and watching for neurologic and cardiovascular signs of LAST.

questions.stem: Which anesthetic is true total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA)?
options: Propofol plus nitrous oxide at 50 percent
Propofol infusion plus sevoflurane at 0.5 MAC
Propofol plus remifentanil, no volatile agent
Sevoflurane alone with IV fentanyl boluses
