questions.explanation: Total intravenous anesthesia means general anesthesia maintained entirely with intravenous drugs, with no volatile agent or nitrous oxide. Propofol provides hypnosis and remifentanil analgesia, making the combination a classic TIVA technique. Adding nitrous oxide or any sevoflurane makes it a balanced, not total intravenous, anesthetic.

questions.stem: Which THREE features favor propofol-based TIVA in a patient with malignant-hyperthermia susceptibility, severe PONV history, and planned evoked-potential monitoring? (Select 3)
options: Ability to measure end-tidal propofol concentration
Long postoperative analgesia from propofol
Avoidance of volatile MH triggers
Less interference with evoked-potential monitoring
Lower PONV risk than volatile-based anesthesia
Lower awareness risk than volatile anesthesia
questions.explanation: Propofol TIVA avoids volatile triggers of malignant hyperthermia, lowers PONV risk, and depresses evoked potentials less than volatile agents. There is no routine end-tidal propofol measurement, awareness risk can actually rise if the IV fails, and propofol provides no lasting analgesia.

questions.stem: What delivery-monitoring limitation is unique to TIVA compared with volatile anesthesia?
options: Capnography cannot be used with an IV technique
Pulse oximetry becomes unreliable with propofol
ECG monitoring is affected by infusion pumps
No end-tidal level confirms the hypnotic arrived
questions.explanation: Unlike volatile anesthesia, routine TIVA provides no measured end-tidal hypnotic concentration confirming delivery to the patient. That makes reliable IV access, pump and line surveillance, and multimodal assessment of depth especially important; processed EEG is an adjunct, not a propofol concentration monitor.

questions.stem: Why can processed EEG be especially useful during fully paralyzed TIVA?
options: Processed EEG measures neuromuscular block depth
Movement can no longer signal light anesthesia
It reports the plasma propofol concentration
It replaces standard physiologic monitoring
questions.explanation: Neuromuscular blockade removes movement as one clinical sign of inadequate anesthesia, which raises awareness risk during TIVA. Processed EEG adds information about hypnotic state, but it does not measure paralysis or plasma propofol concentration and does not replace standard monitoring.

questions.stem: Which pairing provides a common balanced TIVA technique?
options: Dexmedetomidine as the complete anesthetic
Midazolam for analgesia with ketamine for amnesia
Propofol for hypnosis, remifentanil for analgesia
Fospropofol with no added analgesic agent
questions.explanation: Balanced TIVA separates the anesthetic components: propofol provides titratable hypnosis and amnesia, while remifentanil supplies rapidly adjustable opioid analgesia. Their short, titratable effects allow rapid emergence when dosed well. Midazolam has no analgesic action, and dexmedetomidine alone does not reliably provide surgical anesthesia.

questions.stem: Why should longer-acting postoperative analgesia be established before stopping propofol-remifentanil TIVA?
options: Propofol provides hours of analgesia after stopping
Propofol blocks opioid receptors for several hours
Remifentanil effects persist for several hours
Remifentanil offset is fast; propofol is not analgesic
questions.explanation: Remifentanil's effect dissipates within minutes after stopping an infusion, and propofol provides little intrinsic analgesia. Without a longer-acting analgesic strategy established before emergence, the patient can awaken rapidly with severe untreated postoperative pain.

questions.stem: During TIVA, the propofol pump alarms for occlusion while processed EEG values and HR rise. What is the most likely problem?
options: Hypnotic delivery interrupted; awareness risk
Excess propofol delivery from a pump surge
Remifentanil accumulation raising heart rate
Neuromuscular block deepening too far
questions.explanation: An occlusion alarm means programmed pump delivery may not be reaching the patient. Rising processed EEG values and heart rate fit falling anesthetic effect, so the infusion path and IV access should be restored promptly to reduce awareness risk. Excess propofol would lower, not raise, the processed EEG.

questions.stem: During prone TIVA with tucked arms, which IV setup best reduces the risk of unnoticed hypnotic-delivery failure?
options: Hand IV hidden under drapes for stability
Dedicated, visible line with minimal dead space
Shared line also used for boluses and blood
Extra-long extension tubing to reach the pump
questions.explanation: TIVA safety depends on uninterrupted drug delivery because no exhaled anesthetic concentration confirms that the hypnotic is reaching the patient. A dedicated line with visible connections and minimal dead space makes infiltration, disconnection, occlusion, and delayed dose changes easier to detect.

questions.stem: During propofol TIVA, a ketamine bolus is given and the BIS rises from 45 to 62 within minutes, with stable hemodynamics and an intact, visible IV. What is the best interpretation?
options: Ketamine has reversed the propofol hypnosis
The propofol line has just become disconnected
Ketamine raises EEG-based indices despite depth
The patient is now aware and needs more propofol
questions.explanation: Ketamine increases high-frequency EEG activity, so BIS and similar indices can rise even though overall anesthetic depth has increased, and the number must be read alongside the drug history. Ketamine does not antagonize propofol. With a visible, intact line and a rise timed to the bolus, a delivery failure is unlikely.

questions.stem: During TIVA, surgical stimulation suddenly increases. How should drug delivery be adjusted?
options: Raise remifentanil whatever the BP or breathing
Raise propofol based on heart rate by itself
Adjust only to keep a processed-EEG target
Titrate both components to depth and hemodynamics
questions.explanation: TIVA infusions are titrated to patient characteristics, hemodynamics, surgical intensity, and signs of depth rather than to fixed doses or a single number. A sudden rise in stimulation usually needs more antinociception from the opioid, with the hypnotic adjusted to processed EEG and clinical signs, while blood pressure and ventilation are watched.

questions.stem: Core temperature falls from 36.5 to 34 C during spine surgery with stable anesthetic depth. What SSEP change is expected?
options: Increased latency
Decreased latency
No change in latency
Loss of all waveforms
questions.explanation: Cooling slows nerve conduction, so SSEP latency increases roughly in proportion to the temperature drop, and a change caused by hypothermia can be mistaken for neural compromise. Warming reverses it. Shorter latency comes with warming, and mild hypothermia does not abolish waveforms.

questions.stem: MEPs disappear immediately after rocuronium while SSEPs remain unchanged. What best explains the pattern?
options: Rocuronium selectively injures motor tracts
Paralysis blocks the muscle response MEPs record
SSEPs depend on neuromuscular transmission
The pattern points to anterior cord ischemia
questions.explanation: Muscle-recorded MEPs require transmission through the neuromuscular junction to produce a measurable response. Rocuronium blocks that final pathway and can abolish MEPs, while SSEPs do not depend on neuromuscular transmission. Anterior cord ischemia can give the same pattern, but loss immediately after rocuronium points to the drug.

questions.stem: Increasing volatile anesthetic concentration during SSEP monitoring typically causes which change?
options: No change
Increased amplitude and decreased latency
Decreased amplitude and increased latency
Increased amplitude with unchanged latency
questions.explanation: Volatile anesthetics depress cortical and subcortical evoked responses in a dose-dependent fashion, typically reducing SSEP amplitude and prolonging latency. Large or abrupt concentration changes can therefore mimic neurologic deterioration.

questions.stem: If a volatile anesthetic must supplement an evoked-potential anesthetic, what general strategy best preserves signals?
options: At least 1 MAC so awareness risk stays low
Varied doses to test whether signals respond
Lowest stable dose that keeps signals readable
Deep paralysis to improve the MEP amplitude
questions.explanation: Volatile agents suppress evoked potentials in a concentration-dependent manner, especially MEPs. If one must be used, the lowest stable concentration that still provides adequate anesthesia and interpretable signals is preferable to high concentrations or abrupt changes, and paralysis abolishes rather than improves muscle-recorded MEPs.

questions.stem: The surgeon requests deeper paralysis during muscle-recorded MEP monitoring. What is the main anesthetic concern?
options: Paralysis improves MEP amplitude and clarity
Both SSEPs and MEPs require full paralysis
Blockade affects only the sensory pathways
More blockade can abolish MEPs; coordinate first
questions.explanation: Muscle-recorded MEPs require functional neuromuscular transmission, so additional paralysis can reduce or abolish the signal independent of spinal cord function. Neuromuscular blockade after intubation must therefore be minimized or deliberately titrated in coordination with the monitoring team.

questions.stem: SSEPs deteriorate immediately after a large abrupt anesthetic change. What should be considered before concluding neurologic injury occurred?
options: Anesthetic changes alone can alter the signals
SSEPs are unaffected by anesthetic depth
The change proves cord ischemia has occurred
Only equipment failure changes signals abruptly
questions.explanation: Evoked potentials respond not only to neural injury but also to anesthetic concentration, blood pressure, oxygenation, hemoglobin, temperature, and technical factors. A deterioration right after a large anesthetic change should prompt review of that change while surgical and other causes are assessed.

questions.stem: Which FOUR physiologic/anesthetic factors should be checked when evoked-potential signals deteriorate? (Select 4)
options: Increasing the volatile concentration
Blood pressure/perfusion
Oxygenation and hemoglobin
Adding a neuromuscular blocker before MEPs
Recent anesthetic-depth/concentration changes
Temperature
questions.explanation: When evoked potentials deteriorate, perfusion, oxygenation, hemoglobin, temperature, and recent anesthetic changes are reviewed because each can depress signals or mimic neural injury. Increasing volatile concentration depresses signals further, and neuromuscular blockade abolishes muscle-recorded MEPs.

questions.stem: Why is propofol-opioid TIVA commonly favored when both SSEPs and MEPs are important?
options: Propofol raises MEP amplitude above baseline
It depresses signals less than volatile agents
It allows unlimited neuromuscular blockade
It removes the need for blood pressure control
questions.explanation: Propofol-opioid TIVA generally depresses SSEP and especially MEP signals less than clinically significant volatile concentrations. It is therefore commonly chosen when signal quality is critical, while stable dosing and adequate perfusion remain essential and neuromuscular blockade still has to be limited.

questions.stem: During TIVA, processed EEG shows marked burst suppression with hypotension. What should be considered first?
options: Normal depth needing no reassessment
Awareness, so propofol should be increased
Excess hypnotic; reduce depth, support BP
Inadequate neuromuscular blockade
questions.explanation: Marked burst suppression suggests deep cortical depression, and concurrent hypotension raises concern that anesthetic effect is excessive for the patient's current state. The hypnotic should be reassessed and reduced when appropriate while perfusion is supported; the processed EEG number should not be treated without clinical context.

questions.stem: Before induction, a calm awake patient has a processed-EEG index near 95. How should this be interpreted?
options: Consistent with an awake state
Typical general-anesthesia range
Evidence of burst suppression
Evidence of excessive propofol
questions.explanation: Processed-EEG indices near 90–100 are generally consistent with wakefulness, while lower values accompany increasing hypnotic effect. The index is an adjunct and can be affected by artifact, but a calm awake patient near 95 is an expected baseline finding.

questions.stem: Transcranial MEP stimulation causes forceful jaw contraction with each pulse train. Which precaution prevents the injury this causes?
options: A hard oral airway between the incisors
A cervical collar to limit neck movement
Taping the eyes closed with gel pads
Soft bite blocks placed between the molars
questions.explanation: Transcranial stimulation directly activates the temporalis and masseter muscles, so the jaw clenches with each train and can cause tongue and lip lacerations, tooth fractures, or a bitten endotracheal tube. Soft bite blocks between the molars on both sides prevent this, while a hard oral airway between the incisors concentrates force on the teeth. Eye protection matters but addresses a different injury.

questions.stem: When does processed EEG add the most value during TIVA?
options: When paralysis hides clinical signs of depth
When the patient is awake before induction
When it is used in place of standard monitors
When the volatile concentration is already known
questions.explanation: Processed EEG is most useful as an adjunct when the usual clinical signs of hypnotic depth are limited, including TIVA with neuromuscular blockade, because there is also no end-tidal agent level. Its value must be interpreted in the full clinical context alongside standard monitors.

questions.stem: Why does propofol's clinical effect lag behind a sudden increase in its plasma concentration?
options: Time needed to convert propofol to an active form
Equilibration time between plasma and effect site
Slow hepatic uptake delaying plasma levels
Redistribution from fat back into the brain
questions.explanation: The brain behaves as a separate effect-site compartment, and drug must move from plasma into it, a delay described by the ke0 rate constant; for propofol the equilibration half-time is a few minutes. Propofol is active as given, and its hepatic clearance ends rather than delays its effect. Target-controlled infusions briefly overshoot plasma levels to speed that equilibration.

questions.stem: Which THREE practices reduce awareness risk during TIVA with tucked arms? (Select 3)
options: Trust the pump display if no alarm sounds
Rely on an end-tidal propofol concentration
Run propofol through the blood transfusion line
Maintain an observable/reliable dedicated IV pathway
Repeatedly check for infiltration, disconnection, and occlusion
Verify accurate pump programming
questions.explanation: Awareness during TIVA is prevented by verifying pump programming, using a dedicated observable infusion line, and repeatedly checking for infiltration, disconnection, or occlusion, especially when arms are tucked. A pump can show a normal rate while drug infiltrates the tissue, and there is no routine end-tidal propofol measurement.

questions.stem: A patient with a confirmed malignant hyperthermia susceptibility needs general anesthesia for an urgent case. Which plan is appropriate?
options: Sevoflurane, since it is a weak trigger
TIVA with succinylcholine for the RSI
Trigger-free TIVA on a prepared machine
Prophylactic dantrolene, then sevoflurane
questions.explanation: All volatile agents and succinylcholine trigger malignant hyperthermia, so the plan is TIVA with a nondepolarizing relaxer, on a machine flushed or fitted with charcoal filters and with dantrolene available. Prophylactic dantrolene is not recommended and does not make a volatile safe, and sevoflurane is still a trigger.

questions.stem: During spine surgery, MEP amplitudes progressively decline while SSEPs also worsen and mean arterial pressure has fallen substantially. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Rocuronium is selectively depressing SSEPs
The changes prove spinal cord injury occurred
MEPs are unaffected by blood pressure changes
Correct global perfusion before blaming the NMB
questions.explanation: Simultaneous deterioration of MEPs and SSEPs with hypotension suggests a physiologic or perfusion contributor, and neuromuscular blockade cannot explain SSEP loss. The team should correct reversible factors such as blood pressure, oxygenation, ventilation, temperature, and anesthetic effects while coordinating with the surgical and monitoring teams.

questions.stem: During scoliosis correction, MEPs are lost in both legs while SSEPs stay normal. BP, anesthetic depth, and train-of-four are unchanged. Which territory is most likely compromised?
options: Dorsal columns via posterior spinal arteries
Anterior spinal artery to motor tracts
Peripheral nerves at the positioning pads
Neuromuscular junctions from residual block
questions.explanation: MEPs travel in the corticospinal tracts, supplied by the anterior spinal artery, while SSEPs travel in the dorsal columns, supplied by the posterior spinal arteries, so isolated bilateral MEP loss with normal SSEPs points to anterior cord ischemia. An unchanged train-of-four rules out residual blockade, and a positioning nerve injury would be unilateral and affect SSEPs too. Raising MAP and alerting the surgeon come first.

questions.stem: Compared with volatile-based general anesthesia, propofol-based TIVA has what effect on postoperative nausea and vomiting risk?
options: It prevents all PONV
It markedly increases PONV risk
It has no relationship to PONV
It generally reduces PONV risk
questions.explanation: Propofol-based TIVA is associated with less postoperative nausea and vomiting than volatile-anesthetic maintenance, making it useful in patients with high baseline PONV risk. The benefit does not eliminate the need for multimodal prophylaxis when overall risk remains high.

questions.stem: Which BIS range is generally targeted for maintenance of general anesthesia?
questions.explanation: A BIS of 40 to 60 is the usual target for general anesthesia; values above 60 raise concern for possible awareness, and values below 40, especially with burst suppression, suggest more hypnotic than needed. Values from 60 to 90 overlap with sedation and light anesthesia, where recall is possible.

questions.stem: A patient awakens rapidly and smoothly after stopping well-titrated propofol-remifentanil TIVA. Which pharmacologic feature contributed?
options: Propofol has a specific reversal agent
Remifentanil leaves hours of analgesia
TIVA beats every volatile for emergence
Both drugs have short, titratable offsets
questions.explanation: Propofol's short context-sensitive half-time and remifentanil's esterase metabolism, with a half-time of about 3 to 4 minutes, let both fall quickly when stopped, so a well-titrated propofol-remifentanil anesthetic wakes rapidly. Propofol has no reversal agent, and remifentanil leaves almost no residual analgesia, which is why longer-acting analgesia is given before emergence.

questions.stem: After high-dose remifentanil TIVA, a patient has unexpectedly high opioid requirements in PACU. What is the most likely contributor?
options: Opioid-induced hyperalgesia after remifentanil
Accumulation of an active remifentanil metabolite
Propofol antagonizing opioid receptors
Delayed remifentanil release from fat stores
questions.explanation: High-dose remifentanil infusions can cause acute tolerance and opioid-induced hyperalgesia, so pain and opioid requirements after emergence can be higher than expected; ketamine and a longer-acting opioid before emergence help. Remifentanil's metabolite is essentially inactive, the drug does not accumulate in fat, and propofol does not block opioid receptors.

questions.stem: Why can a large IV-line dead space make TIVA titration misleading?
options: Drug delivery becomes faster than programmed
Rate changes reach the patient after a delay
It raises end-tidal propofol concentration
It reduces the risk of infiltration at the site
questions.explanation: Drug already in the IV tubing must traverse the line's dead space before a new pump rate or concentration reaches the circulation. Large dead space therefore delays the clinical effect of a programming change, which can lead to premature repeat adjustments or overshoot.

questions.stem: Which TWO statements correctly distinguish SSEP and MEP monitoring? (Select 2)
options: SSEPs evaluate sensory pathway conduction
MEPs evaluate motor pathway conduction
MEPs are unaffected by neuromuscular blockade
Volatile anesthetics improve both modalities
SSEPs require intact neuromuscular transmission
MEPs are purely sensory
questions.explanation: SSEPs test ascending sensory pathways in the dorsal columns, and MEPs test descending motor pathways and need intact neuromuscular transmission because they are recorded from muscle. Volatile anesthetics depress both, and neuromuscular blockade abolishes muscle MEPs but does not affect SSEPs.

questions.stem: Which anesthetic plan generally best preserves muscle-recorded MEPs during spine surgery?
options: High-dose volatile with deep paralysis
1.5 MAC sevoflurane with a rocuronium drip
Propofol-opioid TIVA with little or no blockade
Nitrous oxide plus volatile with deep paralysis
questions.explanation: Propofol-opioid TIVA generally preserves MEPs better than substantial volatile anesthesia, and avoiding or minimizing neuromuscular blockade preserves the muscle response required for recording. Nitrous oxide also depresses MEPs. Stable anesthetic and physiologic conditions further improve interpretability.

questions.stem: Why are frequent large propofol-rate changes undesirable during critical neuromonitoring periods?
options: Propofol has no effect on evoked potentials at all
Frequent changes improve the reproducibility of signals
Opioids, not propofol, drive evoked potential changes
Depth changes alter signals and cloud interpretation
questions.explanation: Evoked potential amplitude and latency change with anesthetic depth. Frequent large propofol adjustments introduce global signal variability that can obscure or mimic a true neurologic change, so a stable anesthetic is preferred during critical monitoring periods. Opioids have relatively little effect on evoked potentials.

questions.stem: During propofol TIVA with MEP monitoring, the team considers adding 50% nitrous oxide. What effect on MEPs is most likely?
options: Reduced MEP amplitude
Increased MEP amplitude
No effect on MEPs
Effect on SSEP latency only
questions.explanation: Nitrous oxide depresses both SSEPs and MEPs, and added to a propofol technique it reduces MEP amplitude more than its MAC fraction would suggest, so it is usually avoided during critical motor monitoring. It does not enhance signals, and its effect is not limited to SSEPs.

questions.stem: Which anesthetic induction agent can increase cortical SSEP amplitude?
options: Sevoflurane
Etomidate
Midazolam
Thiopental
questions.explanation: Etomidate and ketamine can increase cortical SSEP amplitude, and etomidate infusions have been used to enhance weak signals. Volatile agents, midazolam, and barbiturates all depress amplitude to varying degrees, with volatile agents having the largest effect at clinically used concentrations.

questions.stem: Which TWO features may favor propofol-based TIVA during brain or spine surgery? (Select 2)
options: Compatibility with evoked-potential monitoring
Longer-lasting postoperative analgesia
Lower awareness risk than volatile anesthesia
Removal of the need for arterial monitoring
Ability to deepen with a volatile agent
Reduced PONV risk
questions.explanation: Propofol TIVA depresses evoked potentials less than volatile agents and lowers PONV risk, which suits brain and spine surgery with monitoring. It does not use a volatile agent, does not reduce awareness compared with volatiles, especially if IV delivery fails, and provides no lasting analgesia.

questions.stem: A patient weighs 140 kg with a lean body weight of 70 kg. On which weight should a remifentanil infusion be based?
options: Total body weight
Body surface area
Lean body weight
Twice the ideal body weight
questions.explanation: Remifentanil distributes mainly into lean tissue, and its clearance tracks lean mass, so dosing by total body weight in obesity causes overdose with bradycardia and hypotension. Dosing by lean or ideal body weight matches the actual distribution volume. Body surface area is not used for anesthetic infusions.

questions.stem: Which opioid's context-sensitive half-time is least affected by how long the infusion has run?
options: Fentanyl
Sufentanil
Alfentanil
Remifentanil
questions.explanation: Remifentanil is hydrolyzed by nonspecific blood and tissue esterases, so its context-sensitive half-time stays about 3 to 4 minutes no matter how long it runs. Fentanyl's rises steeply after a few hours, and sufentanil and alfentanil also rise with duration, though less than fentanyl for infusions of several hours.

questions.stem: At about 0.5 MAC sevoflurane, which neuromonitoring signal is most likely to become hard to obtain?
options: Transcranial motor evoked potentials
Cortical SSEPs from the median nerve
Subcortical SSEP waveforms
Brainstem auditory evoked potentials
questions.explanation: Myogenic MEPs are the most sensitive to volatile anesthetics because the agents suppress anterior horn cell synapses as well as cortical activity, and even about 0.5 MAC can make them hard to obtain. Cortical SSEPs are affected less, subcortical SSEP waveforms are fairly resistant, and brainstem auditory evoked potentials are the most resistant to anesthetics.

questions.stem: Closed-claims analyses have historically identified what concern in non-operating-room anesthesia (NORA)?
options: Claims prove NORA is riskier for every patient
Severe respiratory events with catastrophic outcomes
NORA removes respiratory risk for small cases
Smaller procedures can justify reduced monitoring
questions.explanation: Closed claims analyses of NORA have repeatedly highlighted severe respiratory events and catastrophic outcomes in remote procedural settings. They identify recurring failure patterns and system weaknesses, but because the database holds selected medicolegal claims rather than all anesthetics, it cannot give a population complication rate.

questions.stem: A historical closed-claims dataset reports a greater proportion of death among NORA claims than OR claims. What can appropriately be concluded?
options: Each NORA case has twice the OR mortality
The data show that location alone causes death
More severe claims, not a measured death rate
Claim proportions equal population death rates
questions.explanation: A higher proportion of deaths among NORA claims describes the composition and severity of cases that entered that medicolegal dataset. Without a denominator of all NORA and OR anesthetics, the finding cannot establish mortality incidence or a population-level relative risk.

questions.stem: Sedation is planned for a child in the MRI scanner. Which item poses the greatest projectile hazard if brought into the scanner room?
options: Aluminum oxygen cylinder
MR-conditional infusion pump
Plastic bag-valve-mask device
Standard steel oxygen cylinder
questions.explanation: Ferromagnetic objects such as steel oxygen cylinders are pulled into the magnet with lethal force, so only MR-safe or MR-conditional equipment enters the scanner room. Aluminum cylinders, plastic airway devices, and pumps labeled MR-conditional for that field strength are designed for use there.

questions.stem: Historical NORA closed-claims reviews reported aspiration more often than in OR claims. What is the most appropriate use of that finding?
options: Make aspiration prevention a NORA priority
Treat aspiration as the top NORA complication
Assume double the aspiration risk for each patient
Estimate aspiration risk from location by itself
questions.explanation: A higher share of aspiration among NORA claims supports making fasting review, airway protection decisions, suction, and rescue planning explicit priorities outside the OR. Because claims are a selected sample without a denominator, the finding does not show that aspiration is the most common NORA complication or quantify risk for any individual patient.

questions.stem: During MAC outside the OR, which event deserves especially aggressive prevention because it can progress rapidly to catastrophic injury?
options: Nausea without vomiting during the case
Unrecognized respiratory depression
Transient anxiety before the procedure
Brief discomfort during local injection
questions.explanation: Unrecognized respiratory depression can progress from hypoventilation to hypoxemia, bradycardia, and cardiac arrest within minutes. Prevention depends on continuous ventilation monitoring, attention, and immediate rescue. Mild anxiety, nausea, or brief discomfort does not carry the same risk.

questions.stem: A high-risk cardiology procedure is performed in a remote suite. Which complication should the anesthetic plan be particularly prepared to manage in addition to airway events?
options: Contrast-induced nephropathy
LAST from the access-site block
Major hemodynamic instability
Hyperthermia from long fluoroscopy
questions.explanation: Remote cardiology procedures often involve patients with severe heart disease and procedures that can trigger arrhythmias, tamponade, or sudden blood pressure changes, so the plan must cover major hemodynamic instability as well as airway events. Contrast nephropathy develops days later, and the small access-site local anesthetic dose rarely causes toxicity.

questions.stem: In the interventional radiology suite, how does doubling your distance from the radiation source change your exposure?
options: Falls to one half
Falls to one eighth
Stays about the same
Falls to one quarter
questions.explanation: Radiation exposure follows the inverse square law, so doubling the distance from the source cuts exposure to one quarter, which makes distance one of the most effective protections along with time and shielding. Assuming it only halves underestimates the benefit of stepping back from the beam.

questions.stem: Which FOUR lessons are supported by historical NORA closed-claims patterns? (Select 4)
options: Respiratory events require strong prevention and rescue systems
Aspiration deserves explicit attention
Remote-site preparedness should match anesthesia risk
Catastrophic outcomes have occurred in NORA claims
Claims data directly measure current population incidence
NORA location alone proves causation
questions.explanation: NORA closed-claims reviews highlighted respiratory events, aspiration, and catastrophic outcomes, supporting strong preparation and rescue capability outside the OR. Claims data cannot measure true incidence, since they capture only events that led to claims, and they do not prove that location itself causes harm.

questions.stem: In ASA closed claims for anesthesia outside the OR, which location accounted for the largest share of claims?
options: Gastrointestinal endoscopy suites
Cardiac catheterization labs
Interventional radiology suites
MRI and CT scanners
questions.explanation: In ASA closed claims for remote locations, the GI suite accounted for the largest share, followed by the cardiology labs, with oversedation during MAC as a recurring mechanism. Radiology and MRI claims were less frequent. The pattern points to high-volume endoscopy sedation as a place where monitoring and vigilance failures cluster.

questions.stem: Capnography shows apnea before SpO2 falls during propofol sedation. Which action most directly interrupts progression toward hypoxic arrest?
options: Silence the alarm and follow the SpO2 trend instead
Act on the ventilation change and restore airflow
Raise oxygen flow without addressing the apnea
Wait for SpO2 to fall before intervening
questions.explanation: Capnography shows apnea before SpO2 falls, especially when supplemental oxygen is used. The time to act is at the first ventilation change, by restoring airway patency and ventilation. Waiting for desaturation or only increasing oxygen allows hypoxemia to develop.

questions.stem: Untreated sedation-induced apnea progresses. Which sequence is most physiologically plausible?
options: Immediate hypertension, then ventricular fibrillation
Bradycardia first, then hyperventilation, then apnea
Rising CO2 and falling O2, then bradycardia, then arrest
Better oxygenation, then sudden asystole
questions.explanation: Untreated apnea causes CO2 to rise and oxygenation to fall, followed by bradycardia from hypoxemia and eventually cardiac arrest. The other sequences reverse cause and effect or describe patterns that do not follow from apnea.

questions.stem: During sedation in the MRI suite, the capnography sampling line is about 10 m long. How does this affect the capnogram?
options: Values read falsely high from RF heating
Capnography cannot be used in the scanner
The trace becomes more sensitive to apnea
The trace lags behind the patient's breathing
questions.explanation: Long sampling lines add transit time, so the capnogram lags each breath by several seconds and the waveform may be damped, but it still detects apnea and trends. MR-conditional capnography is standard during MRI sedation. Longer lines do not make readings falsely high or improve sensitivity.

questions.stem: During sedation in CT, minutes after IV contrast, the patient develops hives, wheezing, and BP 70/40. Which drug comes first?
options: Epinephrine
Diphenhydramine
Methylprednisolone
Albuterol
questions.explanation: Hypotension with wheezing and hives after contrast is anaphylaxis, and epinephrine is first-line because it reverses vasodilation, bronchospasm, and mediator release. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts that act too slowly to treat shock, and albuterol treats bronchospasm but not hypotension.

questions.stem: A sedated patient deteriorates during transport between monitored locations. Which system design best prevents this gap?
options: A larger pretransport dose so movement is calm
Monitored transport with rescue-capable staff
Fast transport, skipping monitors to save time
Monitoring restarted once the patient arrives
questions.explanation: The safest system keeps monitoring and rescue capability with the patient throughout transport, including appropriate monitors and personnel who can manage the airway and support ventilation. Moving quickly without monitoring increases the chance that deterioration goes unrecognized, and a larger sedative dose adds to the risk.

questions.stem: Which patient profile has the least reserve for an episode of sedation-induced hypoventilation during transport?
options: Healthy adult with normal heart and lungs
Controlled hypothyroidism on levothyroxine
Recent pulmonary edema with severe CAD
Remote uncomplicated appendectomy at age 20
questions.explanation: Heart failure with recent pulmonary edema and coronary disease leaves little reserve for hypoxemia, hypercarbia, or hemodynamic stress, so even a brief episode of hypoventilation can lead to rapid decompensation. Healthy patients and those with controlled minor conditions tolerate the same event better.

questions.stem: After midazolam, a patient with EF 20% is laid flat for a procedure. SpO2 falls to 88%, RR rises to 30, BP is 170/100, and bilateral crackles appear. What is the most likely cause?
options: Acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema
Hypoventilation from sedative effect
Aspiration of gastric contents
Bronchospasm from airway irritation
questions.explanation: Lying flat increases venous return to a failing left ventricle, and crackles, tachypnea, hypertension, and hypoxemia fit acute pulmonary edema. Sedative hypoventilation would slow the rate rather than drive it to 30, and bronchospasm would cause wheezing rather than crackles. Sitting the patient up, oxygen, and preload or afterload reduction come first.

questions.stem: After midazolam is given in holding, the patient is moved to the procedure room. Which principle applies?
options: Monitoring can begin when the procedure starts
Monitoring and rescue readiness continue in transit
Drug-related risk pauses while the patient is moving
A normal pretransport SpO2 rules out later risk
questions.explanation: The risk of respiratory depression continues after midazolam is given, including during transport. Monitoring and the ability to rescue must continue until the patient reaches the next monitored setting. A normal SpO2 before transport does not predict what will happen once the drug peaks.

questions.stem: During sedation, a patient with severe CAD develops ETCO2 70 mmHg, HR 120/min, and new ST depression. What most directly addresses the cause?
options: Give esmolol first to slow the heart rate
Give nitroglycerin and deepen the sedation
Restore ventilation and correct the hypercapnia
Increase oxygen flow and continue the case
questions.explanation: Hypercapnia from sedative hypoventilation stimulates sympathetic outflow, raising heart rate and myocardial oxygen demand, and the ST depression shows the ischemia that follows. Restoring ventilation removes the cause. A beta-blocker treats the tachycardia but leaves the driver in place, and deeper sedation would worsen ventilation further.

questions.stem: In closed claims for respiratory injury during anesthesia outside the OR, which monitor was most often not in use?
options: Pulse oximetry
Electrocardiography
Noninvasive BP
Capnography
questions.explanation: Respiratory events in remote-location claims, often from oversedation during MAC, frequently occurred without capnography in use, and reviewers judged many preventable with better ventilation monitoring. Pulse oximetry, ECG, and blood pressure were usually present, which is why SpO2 on supplemental oxygen alone failed to warn early.

questions.stem: Which behavior most directly prevents a vigilance-related sedation event?
options: Watch the patient and data; act on early changes
Rely mainly on SpO2 alarms to prompt attention
Lower alarm sensitivity to cut nuisance alarms
Check monitors closely once stimulation begins
questions.explanation: Preventing vigilance-related events depends on continuously watching the patient and monitors and responding promptly to meaningful changes. Relying mainly on SpO2 or turning down alarms delays recognition of hypoventilation, and respiratory depression often appears when stimulation is low, not high.

questions.stem: A cataract patient has OSA, a potentially difficult airway, and restricted access beneath surgical drapes. Which approach best minimizes airway risk if topical anesthesia is adequate?
options: Remifentanil infusion titrated until unresponsive
Lightest effective sedation, keeping cooperation
Deep propofol sedation so the patient cannot move
Neuromuscular blockade with an unsecured airway
questions.explanation: If topical anesthesia controls pain, the safest plan uses the lightest sedation that keeps the patient calm and cooperative while maintaining spontaneous ventilation. Deep sedation increases obstruction risk in OSA, and drapes make airway rescue harder.

questions.stem: Why is deep sedation particularly hazardous during cataract surgery in a patient with OSA and difficult rescue access?
options: OSA lowers the patient's sensitivity to sedatives
Cataract surgery produces intense visceral pain
Lost pharyngeal tone causes obstruction under drapes
Deep sedation relieves OSA airway obstruction
questions.explanation: Deep sedation reduces pharyngeal muscle tone, which causes airway obstruction, especially in OSA, and drapes and the surgical field limit quick access for rescue. OSA patients are more, not less, sensitive to sedatives, and cataract surgery is usually not intensely painful.

questions.stem: During a retrobulbar block for cataract surgery, heart rate abruptly falls from 70 to 35/min. What is the first action?
options: Give atropine before anything else
Deepen sedation to blunt the reflex
Begin transcutaneous pacing at once
Ask the surgeon to stop the stimulus
questions.explanation: Bradycardia during retrobulbar injection or globe pressure is the oculocardiac reflex, with trigeminal afferents and vagal efferents, and stopping the stimulus usually ends it. Atropine is given if bradycardia persists or recurs. Deeper sedation does not block the reflex, and pacing is not needed for a reflex that resolves once stimulation stops.

questions.stem: Light sedation is planned for excision of a facial lesion with electrocautery. On room air the patient's SpO2 is 96% and breathing is unlabored. How should oxygen be managed?
options: Routine 4 L/min by nasal cannula
Room air or the lowest FiO2 needed
Raise flow to 6 L/min for a reserve
100% O2 by mask under the drapes
questions.explanation: ASA fire guidance is to use room air or the lowest oxygen concentration that keeps saturation acceptable during head and neck procedures with an ignition source. A patient at 96% on room air needs no supplemental flow, and routine or extra oxygen enriches the space under the drapes. A mask under the drapes concentrates oxygen beside the cautery tip.

questions.stem: During propofol sedation for colonoscopy, which part of the procedure is usually the most stimulating?
options: Initial rectal insertion of the scope
Slow withdrawal while inspecting mucosa
Looping at the sigmoid and splenic flexure
Cold-snare biopsy of a small polyp
questions.explanation: Stretching the mesentery as the scope forms loops in the sigmoid colon and passes the flexures produces the most intense visceral pain, so sedation needs peak there and fall during withdrawal, when stimulation is low and oversedation becomes the risk. Mucosal biopsy is nearly painless because the colon lining lacks somatic pain fibers.

questions.stem: A healthy patient finished the last dose of a clear-liquid bowel prep 2 hours before deep propofol sedation for colonoscopy and has had no solids for 8 hours. How should fasting status be judged?
options: Adequate; clear liquids need 2 hours
Inadequate; the prep needs 6 hours
Inadequate; any liquid needs 8 hours
Adequate only if the case is under MAC
questions.explanation: ASA fasting guidance allows clear liquids up to 2 hours before sedation or anesthesia, and a clear bowel prep counts as a clear liquid, so this patient is adequately fasted. The 6-hour interval applies to a light meal or nonhuman milk, and fasting rules apply the same way to MAC as to general anesthesia.

questions.stem: Midway through deep propofol sedation for colonoscopy, the patient is rolled from left lateral to supine. What airway change is most likely?
options: Improved FRC and oxygen reserve
Worsened upper-airway obstruction
Less need for jaw support
Lower risk of aspiration
questions.explanation: In the left lateral position, gravity keeps the tongue off the posterior pharynx and lets secretions drain, so rolling a deeply sedated patient supine often brings back snoring and obstruction. Supine positioning lowers FRC rather than improving it and makes regurgitated material more likely to reach the larynx.

questions.stem: High-flow nasal oxygen is used instead of a standard cannula during deep propofol sedation for EGD. Which benefit is best supported?
options: It removes the need for capnography
It prevents aspiration of gastric contents
Fewer desaturation episodes during sedation
It reverses opioid-induced hypoventilation
questions.explanation: High-flow nasal oxygen provides a high FiO2 with some positive airway pressure and dead-space washout, and trials in propofol-sedated endoscopy show fewer desaturation episodes than with a standard cannula. It does not protect against aspiration, treat central hypoventilation, or replace capnography.

questions.stem: Which combination most directly increases aspiration concern before EGD?
options: Controlled hypertension in an older adult
A Mallampati IV view as the only finding
OSA without any gastrointestinal symptoms
Active regurgitation with slow gastric emptying
questions.explanation: Active regurgitation shows that gastric contents are already reaching the upper airway, and delayed gastric emptying means the stomach may still be full, so that combination raises aspiration concern most directly. Mallampati IV and OSA predict difficult rescue rather than aspiration, and hypertension and age do not.

questions.stem: Which TWO findings primarily increase airway-rescue difficulty during deep sedation for EGD? (Select 2)
options: Mild preprocedure anxiety
Mallampati IV with limited mouth opening
Controlled hypertension
Controlled hypothyroidism
Severe OSA
Moderate iron deficiency anemia
questions.explanation: Severe OSA makes the airway likely to collapse, and Mallampati IV with limited mouth opening makes mask ventilation and intubation harder if rescue is needed. Well-controlled thyroid disease and hypertension, mild anxiety, and moderate anemia matter for other reasons but do not make airway rescue harder.

questions.stem: A healthy patient undergoes carpal-tunnel release with effective wide-awake local anesthesia and has only mild anxiety. Which anesthetic strategy best preserves the advantages of the technique?
options: Propofol-remifentanil TIVA with an unsecured airway
Deep propofol sedation
General anesthesia solely for amnesia
Local anesthesia with minimal or no systemic sedation
questions.explanation: Wide-awake local anesthesia works best when the patient stays alert, cooperative, and safe without systemic sedation. With good local anesthesia and only mild anxiety, minimal or no sedation preserves those advantages. Deep sedation or general anesthesia adds risk without clear benefit.

questions.stem: Before a minimally sedated wide-awake hand procedure, which expectation is most important to set?
options: They may hear, see, and remember parts of it
They should expect a breathing tube to be placed
They will have complete amnesia afterward
Paralysis will keep the hand perfectly still
questions.explanation: With minimal sedation, patients may hear conversation, see parts of the environment, and remember the procedure. Setting that expectation beforehand prevents surprise and dissatisfaction. Complete amnesia is not guaranteed at this level, and wide-awake hand surgery relies on the patient moving the hand on request.

questions.stem: A female nonsmoker with prior PONV will receive opioids after lumpectomy. How many simplified Apfel risk factors does she have?
options: Three
Four
Two
Five
questions.explanation: The simplified Apfel score counts female sex, nonsmoking status, a history of PONV or motion sickness, and planned postoperative opioids, so she has all four, predicting roughly an 80% PONV risk. That calls for multimodal prophylaxis such as TIVA, dexamethasone, and a 5-HT3 antagonist. Age and type of surgery are not part of the simplified score.

questions.stem: Why can a regional block improve a general-anesthetic plan for lumpectomy in a patient with cardiac disease and prior PONV?
options: It allows hypotension to be safely ignored
It ensures there will be no PONV afterward
It reduces opioid needs and related side effects
It removes the need for GA in most patients
questions.explanation: A regional block can provide strong analgesia and reduce the need for opioids, which lowers the risk of opioid-related nausea and other side effects, and it reduces pain-driven stress in a patient with heart disease. It does not guarantee freedom from PONV or remove the need for general anesthesia.

questions.stem: During induction for lumpectomy, which comorbidity most directly increases concern about a large propofol bolus causing hypotension?
options: Age by itself without physiologic context
Prior PONV after two previous anesthetics
Stage 3 CKD with normal volume status
Reduced ejection fraction with coronary disease
questions.explanation: A large propofol bolus reduces vascular tone and can lower cardiac output. In a patient with reduced ejection fraction and coronary disease, that can cause marked hypotension and ischemia. Prior PONV and moderate CKD do not have the same effect on induction hemodynamics.

questions.stem: A severely claustrophobic patient who failed oral anxiolysis must lie prone and motionless for a long MRI. Which feature most pushes the plan toward deep anesthesia with full rescue capability?
options: Immobility, prone position, and limited access
MRI scanning is an intensely painful procedure
Claustrophobia lowers the respiratory risk
Prone positioning makes airway rescue easier
questions.explanation: A prolonged MRI that requires prone positioning and complete immobility, with limited access to the airway inside the bore, makes deep anesthesia with a reliable rescue plan more appropriate. Claustrophobia drives the need for sedation, but position and access drive the level of preparation. MRI itself is not painful.

questions.stem: Which THREE features make deep MRI sedation especially challenging? (Select 3)
options: Need for neuromuscular blockade
Remote procedural environment
Intense painful stimulation
Prone positioning
Restricted airway access in the scanner
Large expected blood loss
questions.explanation: Deep MRI sedation is challenging because the airway is hard to reach inside the bore, the location is remote from usual OR resources, and prone positioning makes rescue more difficult. MRI scanning is not painful, needs no paralysis, and involves no blood loss.

questions.stem: During sedation in the MRI scanner, the ECG shows ST elevation and tall T waves in a calm patient with stable vital signs. What is the most likely cause?
options: Myocardial ischemia from sedation
Blood flow in the magnetic field
Hyperkalemia from gadolinium
Pericarditis from RF heating
questions.explanation: Blood, a conductor, flowing through the aorta in the strong static field induces a voltage that adds to the ECG, mainly during the ST segment and T wave, so ST and T changes in the scanner are unreliable for ischemia. Rate and rhythm remain useful. Gadolinium does not cause hyperkalemia, and RF heating does not cause pericarditis.

questions.stem: Which THREE domains form the core of a comprehensive sedation plan? (Select 3)
options: A universal BIS target
Fixed weight-based doses without titration
The proceduralist's preferred sedative
Monitoring and rescue planning
Procedure characteristics
Patient selection and comorbidity
questions.explanation: A safe sedation plan starts with who the patient is, what the procedure demands, and how ventilation will be monitored and rescued, which then shapes drug choice and depth. A proceduralist's preferred drug, rigid weight-based dosing without titration, and a universal BIS target do not address the risks that cause sedation harm.

questions.stem: During propofol colonoscopy MAC, the patient becomes apneic. What is the immediate priority?
options: Increase propofol so the patient stays still
Give flumazenil to reverse the propofol effect
Stop propofol and restore airway and ventilation
Wait for SpO2 to drop before intervening at all
questions.explanation: Apnea during propofol sedation is treated by stopping or reducing propofol and restoring the airway and ventilation, using jaw thrust or bag-mask ventilation as needed. Flumazenil does not reverse propofol, and waiting for desaturation delays treatment.

questions.stem: A cataract patient becomes agitated beneath the drapes. What should be assessed before reflexively deepening sedation?
options: Blood pressure alone, then deepen sedation
Whether the surgeon wants more sedation
Whether paralysis is needed to stop movement
Ventilation, pain, position, and anxiety
questions.explanation: Agitation under drapes can come from hypoxemia, hypercarbia, pain, positioning discomfort, or anxiety. Checking for these causes first avoids deepening sedation when the real problem is ventilation or pain, and more sedation can make some of these problems worse.

questions.stem: During propofol sedation for EGD with the scope and bite block in place, snoring and obstruction develop. Which rescue step fits this shared airway first?
options: Jaw thrust or a nasal airway alongside the scope
Insert an oral airway beside the bite block
Remove the scope and place an LMA immediately
Deepen propofol so the snoring settles down
questions.explanation: With the endoscope and bite block in the mouth, an oral airway cannot be placed, so jaw thrust and a nasopharyngeal airway are the first tools for obstruction and may let the procedure continue. Removing the scope for an LMA is the step if those fail or SpO2 keeps falling, and deeper sedation worsens obstruction.

questions.stem: A Bier block with lidocaine is used for a 15-minute hand procedure. When is cuff deflation first considered safe?
options: Right after the 15-minute case ends
After about 20 minutes, in cycles
After 5 minutes once the hand is numb
Only after 90 minutes have passed
questions.explanation: A Bier block places a large lidocaine dose in the isolated arm, and releasing the cuff before about 20 minutes lets unbound drug wash into the circulation and cause LAST. Between 20 and 40 minutes, cycled deflation with brief reinflation spreads out the bolus. Finishing a 15-minute case does not make early release safe, and waiting 90 minutes only adds tourniquet pain.

questions.stem: A patient undergoing lumpectomy states that remaining aware is unacceptable. How should this preference be incorporated?
options: Treat depth as a purely procedural decision
Promise amnesia under light MAC sedation
Choose a plan that can meet the agreed goal
Use minimal sedation without discussing it
questions.explanation: If the patient does not want to be aware, the anesthesia plan must be able to meet that goal. That requires discussing options and choosing a technique, such as general anesthesia if needed, that achieves the agreed level of consciousness while managing risk. Promising amnesia under light MAC would not be reliable.

questions.stem: What equipment constraint is specific to anesthesia care in the MRI environment?
options: Airway gear is unnecessary since MRI is painless
Standard OR equipment can sit beside the magnet
Monitors must be removed during image acquisition
Gear must be MR-safe or kept outside restricted zones
questions.explanation: MRI safety requires equipment that is MR-safe or MR-conditional for the magnetic environment and monitoring that remains visible despite separation from the patient. Airway and resuscitation planning must also account for removing the patient from the bore before some interventions.

questions.stem: An endoscopist requests deep sedation for a patient with severe OSA, active regurgitation, and a predicted difficult airway. What should determine the final anesthetic plan?
options: The anesthesia provider's integrated risk assessment
The proceduralist's preferred depth of sedation
The patient's stated wish to be completely asleep
The routine practice used for low-risk EGD patients
questions.explanation: Severe OSA, active regurgitation, and a predicted difficult airway materially change the risk of deep sedation with an unsecured airway. The final plan should integrate aspiration risk, rescue difficulty, procedural needs, and patient goals rather than follow the proceduralist's depth preference or routine practice.

questions.stem: For colonoscopy, why is a titratable hypnotic often paired with analgesic/local strategies rather than simply maximizing hypnotic dose?
options: Hypnotics by themselves provide full analgesia
Pain and hypnosis differ; more hypnotic adds risk
Opioids remove the respiratory risk of sedation
Colonoscopy requires general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Propofol produces hypnosis but no analgesia, so pushing it higher to cover visceral pain from scope looping trades discomfort for apnea and hypotension. Pairing a titratable hypnotic with a small opioid dose or another analgesic strategy covers both components at lower doses of each. Opioids add respiratory depression rather than removing it.

questions.stem: Why is oversedation during cataract surgery under topical anesthesia hazardous to the eye itself?
options: Sedatives raise intraocular pressure markedly
Deep sedation constricts the pupil during surgery
Disoriented arousal can cause sudden head movement
Topical anesthetic wears off faster when sedated
questions.explanation: Deeply sedated patients may snore, obstruct, or wake disoriented and move suddenly, and a jerk of the head during intraocular work can cause serious injury such as posterior capsule rupture. Light sedation with a cooperative patient is safer for the eye as well as the airway. Common sedatives lower or barely change intraocular pressure, and sedation does not shorten topical anesthesia.

questions.stem: After midazolam and fentanyl, RR falls to 5/min and ETCO2 rises while the patient remains arousable. What is the immediate priority before deciding on an antagonist?
options: Observe, since talking rules out hypoventilation
Give naloxone before assessing ventilation
Give flumazenil, since arousal rules out opioids
Support ventilation, then titrate reversal
questions.explanation: A rate of 5 with rising ETCO2 is hypoventilation even in a patient who still talks, so airway and ventilation support come first. Because the slow rate fits opioid effect, naloxone is then titrated, with flumazenil considered if benzodiazepine sedation persists. Arousability does not exclude dangerous CO2 retention.

questions.stem: Flumazenil is chosen to reverse benzodiazepine oversedation. Which dosing approach is standard?
options: 0.2 mg IV every minute to effect, up to 1 mg
0.4 mg IV once, repeated every 2 hours
2 mg IV bolus for complete reversal
40 mcg IV every 2 minutes to effect
questions.explanation: Flumazenil is titrated as 0.2 mg IV over 15 seconds, repeated every minute to effect, up to about 1 mg, which limits withdrawal and seizure risk. Its effect lasts about an hour, so the patient is observed for resedation. Doses of 40 mcg describe dilute naloxone titration, and a 2 mg bolus exceeds what is needed and raises seizure risk.

questions.stem: Propofol causes apnea and a colleague reaches for flumazenil. What is the correct response?
options: Give flumazenil, since it reverses most sedatives
Flumazenil cannot reverse propofol; ventilate
Give naloxone, which reverses propofol apnea
Delay ventilation until propofol redistributes
questions.explanation: Flumazenil acts only at the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptors, and propofol has no reversal agent, so apnea after propofol is treated by supporting the airway and ventilating until redistribution ends the effect, usually within minutes. Naloxone reverses opioids only, and delaying ventilation risks hypoxemia.

questions.stem: A child had severe emergence delirium after a prior sevoflurane anesthetic. Which adjunct most reduces the chance of recurrence?
options: Midazolam premedication by itself
Extra sevoflurane during emergence
Dexmedetomidine before emergence
Physostigmine at the end of surgery
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine given intraoperatively reduces emergence delirium after sevoflurane in children, providing sedation and some analgesia without respiratory depression. Midazolam premedication does not reliably prevent it and may add postoperative confusion, deepening sevoflurane only delays the same emergence, and physostigmine is for central anticholinergic syndrome.

questions.stem: Compared with propofol alone, how does a ketamine-propofol combination for a brief painful procedure tend to affect the patient?
options: More hypotension from additive vasodilation
Complete freedom from respiratory events
More emergence agitation than ketamine alone
Less hypotension at similar sedation depth
questions.explanation: Ketamine's sympathetic stimulation offsets propofol's vasodilation, and studies of ketamine-propofol combinations show less hypotension than propofol alone at comparable sedation. Respiratory events still occur, and propofol tends to reduce, not increase, ketamine emergence reactions compared with ketamine alone.

questions.stem: During TIVA with MEP monitoring, bilateral signals fall immediately after a large propofol bolus while MAP, oxygenation, temperature, and hemoglobin remain stable. What should be considered first?
options: A global anesthetic effect from the abrupt depth change
A focal surgical injury at the instrumented level
Neuromuscular blockade wearing off during the case
Unilateral cord ischemia from a misplaced screw
questions.explanation: Anesthetic effects usually alter neuromonitoring globally rather than unilaterally. Because the bilateral MEP decrease immediately followed a large propofol bolus while perfusion, oxygenation, temperature, and hemoglobin stayed stable, the abrupt increase in depth is the leading reversible explanation while surgical and technical causes are reviewed. Blockade wearing off would raise, not lower, MEPs.

questions.stem: During TIVA, only left-sided MEPs deteriorate immediately after pedicle-screw placement while anesthetic depth and physiology remain unchanged. What requires urgent evaluation?
options: A global propofol depth effect
A focal surgical/neurologic cause
Systemic hypotension from blood loss
Global hypothermia slowing conduction
questions.explanation: A unilateral MEP loss immediately after pedicle-screw placement is anatomically and temporally more concerning for a focal surgical or neurologic problem than for a systemic effect. Anesthetic depth, hypotension, and hypothermia act globally and would affect both sides, although technical causes should also be checked urgently.

questions.stem: A patient susceptible to malignant hyperthermia requires spine surgery with muscle-recorded MEPs. Which plan best satisfies both constraints?
options: Desflurane maintenance with prophylactic dantrolene
Sevoflurane with a continuous rocuronium infusion
Trigger-free TIVA with minimal blockade after intubation
Isoflurane with deep paralysis for the exposure
questions.explanation: MH susceptibility requires avoiding volatile anesthetics and succinylcholine, while muscle-recorded MEPs require intact neuromuscular transmission. Propofol-opioid TIVA satisfies the trigger-free requirement and generally preserves evoked potentials, with neuromuscular blockade minimized after intubation. Prophylactic dantrolene does not make a volatile agent acceptable.

questions.stem: During propofol-remifentanil TIVA, processed EEG remains in the intended hypnotic range but HR and BP surge at incision. Which component most likely needs adjustment?
options: Hypnosis, by raising the propofol
Neuromuscular block depth
Volume, with a fluid bolus first
Antinociception, such as remifentanil
questions.explanation: Processed EEG reflects hypnotic state but not nociception, so a heart rate and blood pressure surge at incision with an on-target index points to inadequate antinociception, which is treated by increasing remifentanil. Raising propofol deepens hypnosis without fixing the cause and adds hypotension, and paralysis or fluid does not address a pain response.

questions.stem: Propofol-remifentanil TIVA is ending after an open abdominal case with no regional block. Which analgesic transition plan is best?
options: Longer-acting opioid 20 to 30 minutes before the end
Longer-acting opioid once the patient is extubated
Increase remifentanil just before stopping it
Rely on propofol's residual analgesic effect
questions.explanation: A longer-acting opioid such as morphine or hydromorphone needs time to reach peak effect, so giving it 20 to 30 minutes before remifentanil stops, with multimodal adjuncts, covers the gap when remifentanil wears off within minutes. Waiting until extubation leaves the patient in pain during the onset delay, and propofol has no residual analgesic effect.

questions.stem: A failed field block causes pain and movement; repeated propofol boluses then produce apnea. What management error occurred?
options: Too little propofol was given for the stimulus
Pain was treated with hypnosis instead of analgesia
Conversion to GA was considered much too early
The block used an excessive local anesthetic dose
questions.explanation: Propofol treats hypnosis, not the nociception left by a failed block. Repeatedly deepening hypnosis to suppress pain-driven movement can cross into apnea or general anesthesia depth without providing analgesia, so the block or analgesic plan should be corrected or the anesthetic converted.

questions.stem: A patient with a large brain tumor is sedated for a stereotactic biopsy, and ETCO2 rises from 40 to 60 mmHg. Why is this especially dangerous?
options: Cerebral vasoconstriction reduces brain blood flow
Hypercapnia sharply lowers the seizure threshold
Cerebral vasodilation raises intracranial pressure
Rising CO2 shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve left
questions.explanation: Cerebral blood flow rises about 1 to 2 mL/100 g/min for each 1 mmHg rise in PaCO2 within the physiologic range, so a 20 mmHg rise markedly increases cerebral blood volume and can push intracranial pressure up in a patient with a mass. Hypercapnia causes vasodilation, not vasoconstriction, and it shifts the oxyhemoglobin curve to the right.

questions.stem: During colonoscopy MAC, the capnography apnea alarm sounds while the provider is charting. What should happen first?
options: Wait for SpO2 to fall to confirm a real event
Finish the charting first, then inspect the waveform
Increase propofol in case the patient is moving
Assess the patient and breathing, then the signal
questions.explanation: A capnography apnea alarm can represent true apnea, obstruction, or a sampling problem, and supplemental oxygen may delay desaturation. The provider should immediately assess the patient and ventilation first, then verify the monitor signal rather than finishing documentation.

questions.stem: After midazolam and fentanyl, a patient is arousable but RR is 6/min. Naloxone is chosen. Which dosing approach is best?
options: Titrate 40 mcg doses to restore breathing
Give 0.4 mg at once for full reversal
Give 2 mg IM and observe for 10 minutes
Give flumazenil first, then naloxone
questions.explanation: Small naloxone increments, such as 40 mcg every 2 to 3 minutes, restore respiratory drive while preserving some analgesia and avoiding the abrupt sympathetic surge, pain, and pulmonary edema that full reversal can cause. Naloxone lasts about 30 to 60 minutes, so the patient must be observed for renarcotization after a longer-acting opioid.

questions.stem: A patient with OSA obstructs every time jaw thrust is released during MAC. What does this recurrent pattern suggest?
options: More sedative will improve the pharyngeal tone
Positioning alone is not enough; add an adjunct
Normal SpO2 on oxygen shows the airway is safe
Brief procedures let the obstruction be ignored
questions.explanation: Obstruction that recurs whenever jaw thrust is removed shows that the patient cannot maintain upper-airway patency at the current depth. A persistent need for manual support should prompt an adjunct such as a nasal airway, lighter sedation, or escalation to a more secure airway plan.

questions.stem: A patient with EF 30% becomes profoundly hypotensive during propofol-remifentanil TIVA. What is the best immediate anesthetic response?
options: Increase remifentanil to blunt the stress response
Increase propofol, since depth may be too light
Cut anesthetic doses, find the cause, support BP
Ignore it while the processed EEG looks right
questions.explanation: Propofol and remifentanil both contribute to hypotension, and an ejection fraction of 30% limits compensatory reserve. Immediate management reduces anesthetic effect when appropriate, looks for other causes such as hypovolemia or bleeding, and restores perfusion with fluids or vasoactive support as indicated.

questions.stem: Which preexisting condition is the strongest reason to avoid dexmedetomidine for procedural sedation?
options: Mild intermittent asthma on albuterol
Obstructive sleep apnea on nightly CPAP
Chronic kidney disease, stage 2
Second-degree AV block without a pacer
questions.explanation: Dexmedetomidine slows sinus and AV nodal conduction through reduced sympathetic tone and increased vagal activity, so preexisting high-grade AV block without a pacemaker can progress to severe bradycardia or asystole. OSA is often a reason to choose it, and mild asthma or early CKD does not limit its use.

questions.stem: A patient aspirated clear gastric fluid during EGD and is now oxygenating adequately with supplemental oxygen. Which management statement is correct?
options: Antibiotics are withheld unless infection develops
Steroids are given routinely to limit lung injury
Saline lavage of the airway dilutes the acid
Broad antibiotics are started immediately for all
questions.explanation: Aspiration pneumonitis is a chemical injury, so antibiotics are not started routinely and are reserved for signs of infection or specific risks such as bowel obstruction. Corticosteroids have not improved outcomes, and saline lavage spreads the acid rather than neutralizing it. Supportive care with suctioning, oxygen, and PEEP when needed is the mainstay.

questions.stem: During ketamine sedation, stridor progresses to silent chest movement with no ETCO2. CPAP with 100% oxygen and jaw thrust fail, and SpO2 is 75%. What is the next step?
options: Give more ketamine to deepen anesthesia
Give a small dose of succinylcholine
Give naloxone and wait two minutes
Give IV lidocaine and keep the CPAP on
questions.explanation: Complete laryngospasm that persists despite CPAP with 100% oxygen and jaw thrust is treated with a small dose of succinylcholine, about 0.1 to 0.5 mg/kg IV, which relaxes the cords; propofol is an alternative only before severe hypoxemia. Naloxone does not act on ketamine, more ketamine does not break the spasm, and IV lidocaine is too slow at an SpO2 of 75%.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis needs a benzodiazepine. Which agent's clearance relies on direct glucuronidation and is least affected by liver disease?
options: Midazolam
Diazepam
Lorazepam
Alprazolam
questions.explanation: Lorazepam, oxazepam, and temazepam undergo direct phase II glucuronidation, which is relatively preserved in cirrhosis, so their clearance changes less than that of drugs needing CYP oxidation. Midazolam, diazepam, and alprazolam all depend on CYP3A4 oxidation and accumulate more in liver disease, and diazepam also has a long-acting active metabolite.

questions.stem: After a large local-anesthetic field infiltration during MAC, the patient develops neurologic symptoms followed by bradycardia and hypotension. What complication should be suspected?
options: Vasovagal reaction to the local injection
Absorbed epinephrine from the local
Anaphylaxis to the local anesthetic
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity
questions.explanation: Neurologic symptoms followed by bradycardia and hypotension after a large local anesthetic dose fit LAST progressing from CNS to cardiovascular toxicity, which calls for airway management, seizure control, and lipid emulsion. Absorbed epinephrine causes tachycardia and hypertension, a vasovagal reaction lacks the neurologic prodrome, and anaphylaxis brings rash and bronchospasm.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient develops hypotension and arrhythmias from local anesthetic systemic toxicity. Which 20% lipid emulsion regimen is standard?
options: 1.5 mL/kg bolus, then 0.25 mL/kg/min
0.5 mL/kg bolus, then 0.025 mL/kg/min
10 mL/kg bolus over 1 minute
3 mL/kg bolus, then 1 mL/kg/min
questions.explanation: For patients 70 kg or less, ASRA recommends 20% lipid emulsion 1.5 mL/kg over 2 to 3 minutes, then 0.25 mL/kg/min, repeating the bolus or doubling the infusion if instability persists, with an upper limit of about 12 mL/kg. Propofol is not a substitute because its lipid content is too low and it depresses the heart.

questions.stem: Why do older patients often reach EEG burst suppression at lower propofol doses than younger adults?
options: Older adults clear propofol much faster
Age increases brain sensitivity to propofol
Processed EEG reads falsely low after age 70
Older patients form more active metabolites
questions.explanation: Brain sensitivity to propofol rises with age while clearance falls, so the same dose produces deeper EEG suppression in older patients, and burst suppression in that group is associated with postoperative delirium. Processed EEG remains usable in older adults, and propofol has no active metabolites.

questions.stem: A healthy 30-year-old is induced with propofol 2 mg/kg. What induction dose is more appropriate for a frail 90-year-old?
options: About 2 mg/kg, as for a young adult
About 3 mg/kg, since clearance is faster
About 1 mg/kg, given slowly
About 0.1 mg/kg in a single push
questions.explanation: Propofol requirements fall with age because of greater brain sensitivity, a smaller central volume, and slower circulation, so a frail 90-year-old often needs about half the young-adult dose, around 1 mg/kg or less, given slowly with time for the peak. A full young-adult dose risks severe hypotension and apnea, and clearance decreases rather than increases with age.

questions.stem: In a patient with renal failure, sedation is prolonged after repeated midazolam doses. What is the main reason?
options: Reduced hepatic CYP3A4 activity from uremia alone
Increased renal reabsorption of parent midazolam
Lower GABA-A receptor density in kidney disease
Accumulation of conjugated alpha-hydroxymidazolam
questions.explanation: Midazolam's main metabolite, alpha-hydroxymidazolam, is active, and its glucuronide also has sedative effect; both are cleared by the kidney, so they accumulate in renal failure and prolong sedation after repeated doses or infusions. Uremia may modestly alter hepatic metabolism, but metabolite accumulation is the main factor.

questions.stem: After rapid high-dose fentanyl, severe chest-wall rigidity makes ventilation ineffective. What is the priority?
options: Ventilate; give a paralytic if rigidity prevents it
Give flumazenil to relax the rigid chest wall
Give more fentanyl to deepen the anesthetic
Apply nasal oxygen and wait for the rigidity to pass
questions.explanation: Opioid-induced rigidity after rapid high-dose fentanyl can make ventilation mechanically ineffective despite an open upper airway. The immediate goal is effective oxygenation and ventilation; severe rigidity may require neuromuscular blockade, with naloxone considered according to the clinical context. Flumazenil has no effect on opioids.

questions.stem: Why must propofol be drawn up aseptically and an opened syringe discarded within about 6 hours?
options: Propofol oxidizes into a toxic compound
Lipid emulsion supports bacterial growth
Light exposure inactivates the drug
Opened vials lose potency within hours
questions.explanation: Propofol's soybean oil and egg lecithin emulsion supports bacterial growth, and contaminated propofol has caused outbreaks of sepsis, so it is drawn up aseptically and syringes are discarded within about 6 hours of opening. Preservatives such as EDTA slow growth but do not keep an opened product sterile. Potency loss and light sensitivity are not the reason.

questions.stem: An MH-susceptible patient will receive TIVA on an anesthesia machine that delivered sevoflurane earlier in the day. How should the machine be prepared?
options: Turn vaporizers off and keep the old circuit
Change the soda lime and nothing else
Charcoal filters on both limbs after a flush
Flush at 2 L/min for 5 minutes by itself
questions.explanation: Activated charcoal filters placed on the inspiratory and expiratory limbs after a brief high-flow flush reduce volatile agent to safe levels within minutes; the alternative is removing vaporizers and flushing at high fresh gas flow per the manufacturer's instructions. Turning vaporizers off leaves agent in the machine and circuit, and a soda lime change or a low-flow flush alone is not enough.

questions.stem: During MAC, a patient becomes restless as ETCO2 rises to 60 mmHg and oxygenation begins to fall. What should be considered before giving more sedative?
options: LAST is the only explanation for this agitation
Agitation shows that hypnosis is insufficient
More sedative will bring the CO2 back down
Hypercapnia and hypoxemia may be driving agitation
questions.explanation: Agitation during sedation is not always inadequate hypnosis. Rising ETCO2 and falling oxygenation indicate worsening ventilation, and hypercapnia and hypoxemia can cause restlessness, so giving more sedative could further depress ventilation and worsen the cause.

questions.stem: During sedation in a patient with asthma, the capnogram develops a slowly sloping upstroke with no clear plateau. What does this pattern indicate?
options: Lower-airway obstruction such as bronchospasm
Partial upper-airway obstruction from the tongue
CO2 rebreathing from an exhausted absorbent
Cardiac oscillations from a slow breathing rate
questions.explanation: A slow, sloping upstroke without a plateau, the shark-fin shape, means alveoli empty unevenly because of lower-airway obstruction, as in bronchospasm or COPD. Upper-airway obstruction more often shrinks and fragments the waveform, rebreathing raises the baseline above zero, and cardiac oscillations are small ripples on the downstroke during slow breathing.

questions.stem: During spine surgery with SSEP monitoring, which anesthetic component has the least effect on SSEPs at usual doses?
options: Nitrous oxide 50%
Remifentanil infusion
Sevoflurane 1 MAC
Isoflurane 0.8 MAC
questions.explanation: Opioids such as remifentanil have minimal effect on SSEP amplitude and latency at clinical doses, which is why opioid-heavy TIVA suits neuromonitoring. Volatile agents near 1 MAC and nitrous oxide both reduce amplitude and prolong latency, and nitrous oxide adds to the suppression from volatile agents.

questions.stem: A patient in the beach-chair position has an arterial line. Where should the transducer be zeroed to best reflect cerebral perfusion?
options: At the level of the right atrium
At the level of the arm cuff
At the external auditory meatus
At the level of the operating table
questions.explanation: Zeroing the transducer at the external auditory meatus, which approximates the circle of Willis, displays pressure at brain level, so hypotension in the upright position is not hidden. Zeroing at the right atrium or the arm reads higher than brain-level pressure by about 0.75 mmHg for every centimeter of height difference.

questions.stem: A cataract MAC patient becomes unresponsive beneath facial drapes. What is the first priority?
options: Wait for SpO2 to fall before lifting drapes
Raise O2 under the drapes and continue surgery
Give more sedative to keep the patient still
Reach the airway and assess breathing directly
questions.explanation: Facial drapes can conceal chest movement and delay access to the airway. When a sedated patient becomes unresponsive, direct assessment of airway patency and ventilation takes priority because obstruction or apnea can progress well before pulse oximetry falls.

questions.stem: A patient becomes apneic while positioned inside the MRI scanner. What should occur immediately?
options: Finish the current sequence, then reassess
Stop imaging and pull the patient out to rescue
Give flumazenil whatever sedative was used
